quote: "And that expression, 'The sword shall devour you [Isaiah 1:20]', does not mean that the disobedient shall be slain by the sword, but the sword of God is fire, of which they who choose to do wickedly become the fuel." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 44
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 44

quote: "But this we assert is inevitable fate, that they who choose the good have worthy rewards, and they who choose the opposite have their merited awards. For not like other things, as trees and quadrupeds, which cannot act by choice, did God make man: for neither would he be worthy of reward or praise did he not of himself choose the good, but were created for this end; nor, if he were evil, would he be worthy of punishment, not being evil of himself, but being able to be nothing else than what he was made." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 43
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 43

quote: "Unless the human race have the power of avoiding evil and choosing good by free choice, they are not accountable for their actions, of whatever kind they be. But that it is by free choice they both walk uprightly and stumble, we thus demonstrate. We see the same man making a transition to opposite things. Now, if it had been fated that he were to be either good or bad, he could never have been capable of both the opposites, nor of so many transitions. But not even would some be good and others bad, since we thus make fate the cause of evil, and exhibit her as acting in opposition to herself; or that which has been already stated would seem to be true, that neither virtue nor vice is anything, but that things are only reckoned good or evil by opinion; which, as the true word shows, is the greatest impiety and wickedness." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 43
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 43

quote: "But lest some suppose, from what has been said by us, that we say that whatever happens, happens by a fatal necessity, because it is foretold as known beforehand, this too we explain. We have learned from the prophets, and we hold it to be true, that punishments, and chastisements, and good rewards, are rendered according to the merit of each man's actions. Since if it be not so, but all things happen by fate, neither is anything at all in our own power. For if it be fated that this man, e.g., be good, and this other evil, neither is the former meritorious nor the latter to be blamed." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 43
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 43

quote: "And the prophecy, ‘binding His foal to the vine, and washing His robe in the blood of the grape [Genesis 49:11],’ was a significant symbol of the things that were to happen to Christ, and of what He was to do. For the foal of an ass stood bound to a vine at the entrance of a village, and He ordered His acquaintances to bring it to Him then; and when it was brought, He mounted and sat upon it, and entered Jerusalem, where was the vast temple of the Jews which was afterwards destroyed by you. And after this He was crucified, that the rest of the prophecy might be fulfilled. For this washing His robe in the blood of the grape was predictive of the passion He was to endure, cleansing by His blood those who believe in Him." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 32
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 32

quote: "In these books...of the prophets we found Jesus our Christ foretold as coming, born of a virgin, growing up to man's estate, and healing every disease and every sickness, and raising the dead, and being hated, and unrecognized, and crucified, and dying, and rising again, and ascending into heaven, and being, and being called, the Son of God." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 31
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 31

quote: "They [i.e., Hebrew Scriptures from the Prophets] had been arranged in books by the prophets themselves in their own Hebrew language. And when Ptolemy king of Egypt formed a library, and endeavored to collect the writings of all men, he heard also of these prophets, and sent to Herod, who was at that time king of the Jews, requesting that the books of the prophets be sent to him. And Herod the king did indeed send them...And when their contents were found to be unintelligible to the Egyptians, he again sent and requested that men be commissioned to translate them into the Greek language. And when this was done, the books remained with the Egyptians, where they are until now. They are also in the possession of all Jews throughout the world; but they, though they read, do not understand what is said." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 31
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 31

quote: "And he [i.e., Marcion], by the aid of the devils, has caused many of every nation to speak blasphemies, and to deny that God is the maker of this universe, and to assert that some other being, greater than He, has done greater works. All who take their opinions from these men, are, as we before said, called Christians." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 26
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 26

quote: "But it [i.e., the Faith] came down to us from the Lord through His disciples. That therefore the ordinances which have been preserved in the Churches from old time until now, may not be lost in our days." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Encyclical Letter, Section 1
reference: Encyclical Letter, Section 1

quote: "The Word Himself was made flesh, and being in the Form of God, took the form of a servant, and from Mary after the flesh became man for us, and that thus in Him the human race is perfectly and wholly delivered from sin and quickened from the dead, and given access to the kingdom of the heavens." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Tome to the Antiochians, Section 7
reference: Tome to the Antiochians, Section 7

quote: "For those who, while pretending to cite the faith confessed at Nicea, venture to blaspheme the Holy Spirit [i.e., by saying the Holy Spirit is a creature and dividing the Trinity], do nothing more than in words deny the Arian heresy while they retain it in thought. But let the impiety of Sabellius and of Paul of Samosata also be anathematized by all, and the madness of Valentinian and Basilides, and the folly of the Manicheans." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Tome to the Antiochians, Section 3
reference: Tome to the Antiochians, Section 3

quote: "But our dwelling is the Church, and our mind ought to be the same. For thus we believe that the Lord also will dwell with us, who says, 'I will dwell with them and walk in them [2 Corinthians 6:16]' and 'Here will I dwell for I have a delight therein [Psalm 132:14].' But by 'here' what is meant but there where one faith and religion is preached?" -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Tome to the Antiochians, Section 1
reference: Tome to the Antiochians, Section 1

quote: "Our teacher of these things [i.e., faith in God, worship of Him, etc.] is Jesus Christ...we reasonably worship Him, having learned that He is the Son of the true God Himself, and holding Him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third, we will prove. For they proclaim our madness to consist in this, that we give to a crucified man a place second to the unchangeable and eternal God, the Creator of all; for they do not discern the mystery that is herein." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 13
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 13

quote: "And when you hear that we look for a kingdom, you suppose without making any inquiry that we speak of a human kingdom." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 11
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 11

quote: "I am amazed at how thou hast called it a 'council,' [i.e., Pyrrhus refers authoritatively to a council called by Sergius in Constantinople about 50 years prior to the 6th Ecumenical Council which addressed Monotheletism/Monoenergism] for it was not held in accordance with conciliar laws and cannons, nor as become ecclesiastical custom, for no encyclical letter was ever issued with the consent of the Patriarchs, nor a place and time of meeting ever established, nor any accuser introduced, nor epistles or delegates sent to any of the other Patriarchs. Those who were introduced were not the proper members for a council, neither bishops, nor metropolitans nor Patriarchs. So how canst thou call this which distributed scandals and discord, throughout the whole world a 'council'?" -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (580-662 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 218
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 218

quote: "If persons be introduced along with the energies...then thou art compelled...either to say that because of the one operation of the Holy Godhead there is one Person as well, or because of its Three Hypostases that there are three operations." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 166
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 166

quote: "If, therefore, the energy be one, as of a whole thing, and what is whole is His hypostasis, then this one energy is hypostatic. Likewise, He must have a different energy than his Father or His Mother, since His hypostasis is different from both of them." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (580-662 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 162
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 162

quote: "So, if according to them [i.e., Monophysites] the Word when He became incarnate did not have this [faculty of will] along with the nature, then I shall never be set free from sin. And if I cannot be freed from sin, then I have not been saved, since 'what is not assumed is not healed [i.e., Saint Gregory Nazianzus, Letter 101]'." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (580-662 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 139
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 139

quote: "Of which part of Him is it said that He thirsted [Matthew 27:34]? If the Godhead, then His Godhead is subject to passion by reason of its desiring drink in a manner contrary to its own nature. If the humanity, then according to that nature with which He thirsted He also willed." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 131
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 131

quote: "If the deification of the will be opposed to the notion that there are two wills, then the deification of the nature excludeth the existence of the two natures." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 116
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 116

quote: "Those who say that there is one will [i.e., in the Person of Christ], whether it be freely-choosing, or gnomic, or self-determining, or whatever else they [i.e., Monophysites] wish to call it...must say whether it be divine, angelic, or human...if they say that this will is divine, then they regard Christ as God alone by nature. If, on the other hand, they say that this will is angelic, then they regard him neither as divine nor human...and if they say that it is human, then they proffer us a mere man." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 101
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 101

quote: "By nature we have an appetite simply for what by nature is good, but we gain experience of the goal in a particular way, through inquiry and counsel. Because of this, then, the gnomic will is fitly ascribed to us being a mode of the employment [of the will], and not a principle of nature, otherwise, nature [itself] would change innumerable times. But the humanity of Christ does not simply subsist [in a manner] similar to us, but divinely, for He Who appeared in the flesh for our sakes was God. It is thus not possible to say that Christ had a gnomic will." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 87
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 87

quote: "The same Person, as man, subjected human nature in Himself, and through Himself, to God the Father, showing Himself as the flawless image and pattern for us to imitate in order that we may voluntarily draw nigh unto God." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 73
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 73

quote: "If man has the faculty of will by nature...and if they [i.e., Monophysites] yet maintain that Christ hath the human will only by mere appropriation of it, then it is necessary for these people to be consistent and to say that His other natural properties are also in Him by mere appropriation of them." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 65
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 65

quote: "So, if natural things be not acquired through teaching, then we have will without having acquired it or being taught it, for no one hath ever had a will which was acquired by teaching...if man was made after the image of the blessed and super-essential Godhead, and if the divine nature be self-determined, then he is by nature endowed with free will...Consequently, man by nature possesseth the faculty of will [i.e., will is proper to nature and not to the person or hypostasis]." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 61
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 61

quote: "If thou sayest there is a synthesis of wills [into one will] then thou shalt be forced to say that there is a synthesis of all other natural properties as well...Long ago, to designate by the term 'nature' [that which resulted from a synthesis of two] natures was heretical [i.e., Anathema 8 of the 5th Ecumenical Council]. Moreover, thou dividest Him from the Father by means of this composite will, for a composite will characterizes only a composite nature." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 27
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 27

quote: "The will and the mode of willing are not the same, just as the power of sight and the mode of perception are not the same. Will, like sight, is of nature. All things which have an identical nature have identical abilities. But the mode of willing, like the mode of perception--in other words...is only a mode of the use of a power of the employment of will and of perception [i.e., will is particular to nature, mode of willing is particular to a person]." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 23
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 23

quote: "If it be not possible for two wills to exist in one and the same person without opposition, then by thine own reasoning [i.e., Saint Maximus is responding to the 'it's impossible for two wills to exist in a person without opposition' argument from Pyrrhus], it is possible with opposition. And if this be possible, then thou hast confessed the existence of two wills. So thou dost not differ over the number of wills, but with a principle of their opposition. So, it remains for us to discover the real cause of this conflict [of wills]. What does thou say this is? The natural will, or sin? If thou sayest it be the natural will, and since we already know that there is no other cause of this than God, then thou makest God the Author of the conflict [of wills]. But if the cause be sin, and if Christ be free from sin, then the Incarnate God hath no opposition of any kind in those wills proper to His natures, since no effect can result from a cause which doth not exist." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 17
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 17

quote: "For if one suggests that a 'willer' is implied in the notion of the will, then by the exact inversion of this principle of reasoning, a will is implied in the notion of a 'willer.' Thus, wilt thou say that because of the one will of the superessential Godhead there is only one hypostasis, as did Sabellius, or that because there are three hypostases there are also three wills, and because of this, three natures as well...?" -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 15
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 15

quote: "Christ existeth as God and as man by nature. Then did He will as God and as man, or only as Christ? If it were Christ, who willed and initiated actions, being both God and man, then it is clear that, being one and the same, He willed dually and not singly. For if Christ be nothing else apart from the natures from which and in which He existeth, then obviously He willeth and operateth in a manner corresponding to each of His natures, in other words, as each nature is capable of operating. And if He hath two natures, then He surely must have two natural wills, the wills and essential operations being equal in number to the natures. For just as the number of natures of the one and the same Christ, correctly understood and explained, doth not divide Christ but rather preserveth the distinction of natures in the union, so likewise the number of essential attributes, wills, and operations attached to those two natures doth not divide Christ either." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 13
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Section 13

quote: "[Pyrrhus:] Dost thou really think that whosoever thinks that there is one will in Christ moves away from Christian doctrine? [Saint Maximus:] Yes, I truly do. For what is a more irreverent conception than that which maintains that the same person with the very same will, which before the Incarnation created everything from nothing and which maintains, provides, and orders everything for salvation, after the Incarnation desireth food and drink, changeth from one position to another, and performeth all manner of similar things that are free from blame and reproach, but which would by this means prove that the whole Economy of the Incarnation was not illusory [i.e., Saint Maximus argues that Monotheletism leads to Docetism--Christ only seemed to have a physical body]?" -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (579-649 AD), The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Sections 6-7
reference: The Disputation with Pyrrhus, Sections 6-7

quote: "But away with the folly of these haters of God and senseless men [i.e., the Arians]. For the Triad, praised, reverenced, and adored, is one and indivisible and without degrees. It is united without confusion...he that blasphemes any one of the Subsistences [i.e., Persons of the Trinity] shall have remission neither in this world nor in that which is to come." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 6
reference: On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 6

quote: "And the Arians torture themselves to no purpose, from not understanding the saying of our Savior, 'All things whatsoever the Father has are Mine.' For from this passage at once the delusion of Sabellius can be upset, and it will expose the folly of our modern Jews." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 5
reference: On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 5

quote: "When...you wish to perceive what relates to the Son, learn what is in the Father, for this is what you must believe to be in the Son. If then the Father is a thing created or made, these qualities belong also to the Son. And if it is permissible to say of the Father 'there was once a time when He was not,' or 'made of nothing,' let these words be applied also to the Son. But if it is impious to ascribe these attributes to the Father, grant that it is impious also to ascribe them to the Son. For what belongs to the Father, belongs to the Son...As then the Father is not a creature, so neither is the Son...But rather, as the Father's attributes are Everlastingness, Immortality, Eternity, and the being no creature, it follows that thus also we must think of the Son." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 4
reference: On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 4

quote: "The Only-begotten from God, Who is by nature inseparable from Him, even though in their madness they [i.e., the Arians] separate Him by their words, not perceiving, the impious men, that the Light can never be separated from the sun, in which it resides by nature." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 3
reference: On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 3

quote: "For it was fitting that while 'through Him' all things came into being at the beginning, 'in Him' (note the change of phrase) all things should be set right [John 1:3 and Ephesians 1:10]. For at the beginning they came into being 'through' Him; but afterwards, all having fallen, the Word has been made Flesh, and put it on, in order that 'in Him' all should be set right. Suffering Himself, He gave us rest, hungering Himself, He nourished us, and going down into Hades He brought us back thence...but at the restoration it was fitting that all things should be 'delivered' to Him, in order that He might be made man, and all things be renewed in Him...that both the judgment of death which hung over us may be delivered to the Son, and that He may then, by dying for us, abolish it for us in Himself." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 2
reference: On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 2

quote: "Since then all things 'were delivered' to Him, and He is made Man, straightway all things were set right and perfected. Earth receives blessing instead of a curse, Paradise was opened to the robber, Hades cowered, the tombs were opened and the dead raised, the gates of Heaven were lifted up to await Him that 'comes from Edom [Psalm 24:7 and Isaiah 63:1]'." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 2
reference: On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 2

quote: "For whereas man sinned, and is fallen, and by his fall all things are in confusion: death prevailed from Adam to Moses [Romans 5:14], the earth was cursed, Hades was opened, Paradise shut, Heaven offended, man, lastly, corrupted and brutalized [Psalm 49:12], while the devil was exulting against us — then God, in His loving-kindness, not willing man made in His own image to perish, said, 'Whom shall I send, and who will go? [Isaiah 6:8]'. But while all held their peace, the Son said, 'Here am I, send Me.' And then it was that, saying 'Go,' He 'delivered' to Him man, that the Word Himself might be made Flesh, and by taking the Flesh, restore it wholly. For to Him, as to a physician, man 'was delivered' to heal the bite of the serpent; as to life, to raise what was dead; as to light, to illumine the darkness; and, because He was Word, to renew the rational nature." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 2
reference: On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 2

quote: "Not even a sparrow falls to the ground without the Father [Matthew 10:29], nor is the grass clothed without God [Matthew 6:30]." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 1
reference: On Luke 10:22 and Matthew 11:27, Section 1

quote: "But it is the part of a Father to beget, while it is a workman's part to create...But the Holy Spirit, being that which proceeds from the Father, is ever in the hands of the Father Who sends and of the Son Who conveys Him, by Whose means He filled all things. The Father, possessing His existence from Himself, begot the Son, as we said, and did not create Him, as a river from a well and as a branch from a root, and as brightness from a light." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Statement of Faith, Section 4
reference: Statement of Faith, Section 4

quote: "Each text then which refers to the creature is written with reference to Jesus in a bodily sense. For the Lord's Humanity was created as 'a beginning of ways,' and He manifested it to us for our salvation. For by it we have our access to the Father. For He is the way (John 14:6) which leads us back to the Father. And a way is a corporeal visible thing, such as is the Lord's humanity." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Statement of Faith, Section 4
reference: Statement of Faith, Section 4

quote: "He is then by nature an Offspring, perfect from the Perfect, begotten before all the hills (Proverbs 8:25), that is before every rational and intelligent essence, as Paul also in another place calls Him 'first-born of all creation' (Colossians 1:15). But by calling Him First-born, He shows that He is not a Creature, but Offspring of the Father. For it would be inconsistent with His deity for Him to be called a creature. For all things were created by the Father through the Son, but the Son alone was eternally begotten from the Father, whence God the Word is 'first-born of all creation,' unchangeable from unchangeable. However, the body which He wore for our sakes is a creature: concerning which Jeremiah says, according to the edition of the seventy translators (Jeremiah 31:22): 'The Lord created for us for a planting a new salvation, in which salvation men shall go about'." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Statement of Faith, Section 3
reference: Statement of Faith, Section 3

quote: "'In Him were all things created, and He is before all' (Colossians 1:16). Now He says not, 'was created' before all things, but 'is' before all things. To be created, namely, is applicable to all things, but 'is before all' applies to the Son only." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Statement of Faith, Section 2
reference: Statement of Faith, Section 2

quote: "But just as a river, produced from a well, is not separate, and yet there are in fact two visible objects and two names. For neither is the Father the Son, nor the Son the Father. For the Father is Father of the Son, and the Son, Son of the Father. For like as the well is not a river, nor the river a well, but both are one and the same water which is conveyed in a channel from the well to the river, so the Father's deity passes into the Son without flow and without division." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Statement of Faith, Section 2
reference: Statement of Faith, Section 2

quote: "For neither do we hold a Son-Father, as do the Sabellians, calling Him of one but not of the same essence, and thus destroying the existence of the Son. Neither do we ascribe the passible body which He bore for the salvation of the whole world to the Father. Neither can we imagine three Subsistences separated from each other, as results from their bodily nature in the case of men, lest we hold a plurality of gods like the heathen." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Statement of Faith, Section 2
reference: Statement of Faith, Section 2

quote: "We believe in one Unbegotten God, Father Almighty, maker of all things both visible and invisible...And in one Only-begotten Word, Wisdom, Son, begotten of the Father without beginning and eternally...also in the Holy Spirit that searches all things, even the deep things of God (1 Corinthians 2:10), and we anathematize doctrines contrary to this." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Statement of Faith, Section 1
reference: Statement of Faith, Section 1

quote: "And [we believe] in one Only-begotten Word, Wisdom, Son, begotten of the Father without beginning and eternally; word not pronounced nor mental, nor an effluence of the Perfect, nor a dividing of the impassible Essence, nor an issue ; but absolutely perfect Son, living and powerful (Hebrews 4:12), the true Image of the Father, equal in honour and glory. For this, he says, 'is the will of the Father, that as they honour the Father, so they may honour the Son also' (John 5:23): very God of very God, as John says in his general Epistles, 'And we are in Him that is true, even in His Son Jesus Christ: this is the true God and everlasting life' (1 John 5:20): Almighty of Almighty. For all things which the Father rules and sways, the Son rules and sways likewise: wholly from the Whole, being like the Father as the Lord says, 'he that has seen Me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). But He was begotten ineffably and incomprehensibly, for 'who shall declare his generation?' (Isaiah 53:8), in other words, no one can. Who, when at the consummation of the ages (Hebrews 9:26), He had descended from the bosom of the Father, took from the undefiled Virgin Mary our humanity, Christ Jesus, whom He delivered of His own will to suffer for us, as the Lord saith: 'No man takes My life from Me. I have power to lay it down, and have power to take it again' (John 10:18)." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Statement of Faith, Section 1
reference: Statement of Faith, Section 1

quote: "For it becomes us who are Christians to turn away from all who speak or think anything against Christ, as being enemies of God, and destroyers of souls; and not even to bid such God speed [2 John 10], lest we become partakers of their sins, as the blessed John has charged us." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), The Deposition of Arius, Section 6
reference: The Deposition of Arius, Section 6

quote: "There have been many heresies before them [i.e., the Arians], which, venturing further than they ought, have fallen into folly; but these men by endeavoring in all their cavils to overthrow the Divinity of the Word...approaching nearer to Antichrist. Wherefore they have been excommunicated and anathematized by the Church. We grieve for their destruction, and especially because, having once been instructed in the doctrines of the Church, they have now sprung away." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), The Deposition of Arius, Section 5
reference: The Deposition of Arius, Section 5

quote: "Who that has heard the words of John, 'In the beginning was the Word [John 1:1]', will not denounce the saying of these men [i.e., Arius and his followers], that 'there was a time when He was not'? Or who that has heard in the Gospel, the 'Only-begotten Son [John 3:16]', and 'by Him were all things made [Colossians 1:16]', will not detest their declaration that He is 'one of the things that were made'...Or again, how is He 'unlike in substance to the Father', seeing He is the perfect 'image and brightness [Hebrews 1:3]' of the Father, and that He says, 'He that has seen Me has seen the Father [John 14:9]'? And if the Son is the 'Word and Wisdom of God [1 Corinthians 1:24]', how was there a 'time when He was not'? It is the same as if they should say that God was once without Word and without Wisdom. And how is He subject to change and variation, Who says, by Himself, 'I am in the Father, and the Father in Me [John 14:11]', and 'I and the Father are One [John 10:30]'; and by the Prophet, 'Behold Me, for I am, and I change not [Malachi 3:6]'? For although one may refer this expression to the Father, yet it may now be more aptly spoken of the Word...as the Apostle has said, 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever [Hebrews 13:8]'." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), The Deposition of Arius, Section 3
reference: The Deposition of Arius, Section 3

quote: "But Eusebius and his fellows admitted them [i.e., Arius and his followers] to communion, being desirous to mingle falsehood with the truth, and impiety with piety. But they will not be able to do so, for the truth must prevail; neither is there any 'communion of light with darkness [2 Corinthians 6:14],' nor any 'concord of Christ with Belial [2 Corinthians 6:15]'." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), The Deposition of Arius, Section 3
reference: The Deposition of Arius, Section 3

quote: "And the novelties they [i.e., the Arians] have invented and put forth contrary to the Scriptures are these following: God was not always a Father, but there was a time when God was not a Father. The Word of God was not always, but originated from things that were not; for God that is, has made him that was not, of that which was not; wherefore there was a time when He was not; for the Son is a creature and a work. Neither is He like in essence to the Father; neither is He the true and natural Word of the Father; neither is He His true Wisdom; but He is one of the things made and created, and is called the Word and Wisdom by an abuse of terms, since He Himself originated by the proper Word of God, and by the Wisdom that is in God, by which God has made not only all other things but Him also. Wherefore He is by nature subject to change and variation as are all rational creatures. And the Word is foreign from the essence of the Father, and is alien and separated therefrom. And the Father cannot be described by the Son, for the Word does not know the Father perfectly and accurately, neither can He see Him perfectly. Moreover, the Son knows not His own essence as it really is; for He is made for us, that God might create us by Him, as by an instrument; and He would not have existed, had not God wished to create us." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), The Deposition of Arius, Section 2
reference: The Deposition of Arius, Section 2

quote: "Now there are gone forth...certain lawless men, enemies of Christ, teaching an apostasy, which one may justly suspect and designate as a forerunner of Antichrist...Eusebius...begins to support these apostates [i.e., Arius and his followers], and has taken upon him to write letters every where in their behalf, if by any means he may draw in certain ignorant persons to this most base and antichristian heresy [i.e., Arianism: Christ was created and not fully divine and of the same essence of the Father]." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), The Deposition of Arius, Section 1
reference: The Deposition of Arius, Section 1

quote: "As there is one body of the Catholic Church, and a command is given us in the sacred Scriptures to preserve the bond of unity and peace." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), The Deposition of Arius, Section 1
reference: The Deposition of Arius, Section 1

topic: On the End of the World
quote: "And then shall appear the signs of the truth; first, the sign of an outspreading in heaven; then the sign of the sound of the trumpet; and the third, the resurrection of the dead; yet not of all, but as it is said: The Lord shall come and all His saints with Him. Then shall the world see the Lord coming upon the clouds of heaven." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 16
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 16

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "They that endure in their faith shall be saved from under the curse itself [i.e., at the end of the age]." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 16
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 16

quote: "Watch for your life's sake. Let not your lamps be quenched, nor your loins unloosed; but be ready, for you know not the hour in which our Lord comes [Matthew 24:42]...for the whole time of your faith will not profit you, if you be not made perfect in the last time." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 16
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 16

quote: "But your prayers and alms and all your deeds so do, as you have it in the Gospel of our Lord." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 15
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 15

quote: "Therefore, appoint for yourselves bishops and deacons worthy of the Lord, men meek, and not lovers of money [1 Timothy 3:4], and truthful and proven; for they also render to you the service of prophets and teachers. Despise them not therefore, for they are your honored ones, together with the prophets and teachers." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 14
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 14

topic: On the Eucharist and Holy Communion
quote: "But every Lord's day gather yourselves together, and break bread, and give thanksgiving after having confessed your transgressions, that your sacrifice may be pure. But let no one that is at variance with his fellow come together with you, until they be reconciled, that your sacrifice may not be profaned. For this is that which was spoken by the Lord: 'In every place and time offer to me a pure sacrifice; for I am a great King, says the Lord, and my name is wonderful among the nations [Malachi 1:11]'." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 15
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 15

quote: "Whosoever, therefore, comes and teaches you all these things that have been said before, receive him. But if the teacher himself turn and teach another doctrine to the destruction of this, hear him not." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 11
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 11

topic: On the Eucharist and Holy Communion
quote: "Now concerning the Thanksgiving (Eucharist), thus give thanks. First, concerning the cup: We thank you, our Father, for the holy vine of David Your servant, which You made known to us through Jesus Your Servant; to You be the glory forever. And concerning the broken bread: We thank You, our Father, for the life and knowledge which You made known to us through Jesus Your Servant; to You be the glory forever. Even as this broken bread was scattered over the hills, and was gathered together and became one, so let Your Church be gathered together from the ends of the earth into Your kingdom; for Yours is the glory and the power through Jesus Christ forever. But let no one eat or drink of your Thanksgiving (Eucharist), but they who have been baptized into the name of the Lord; for concerning this also the Lord has said, Give not that which is holy to the dogs [Matthew 7:6]." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 9
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 9

quote: "Neither pray as the hypocrites; but as the Lord commanded in His Gospel, thus pray: 'Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. Give us today our daily (needful) bread, and forgive us our debt as we also forgive our debtors. And bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one (or, evil); for Yours is the power and the glory forever'. Thrice in the day thus pray." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 8
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 8

quote: "But let not your fasts be with the hypocrites [Matthew 6:16]; for they fast on the second [i.e., Tuesday] and fifth [i.e., Thursday] day of the week; but fast on the fourth day [i.e., Wednesday] and the Preparation (Friday)." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 8
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 8

quote: "And concerning baptism, baptize this way: Having first said all these things, baptize into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [Matthew 28:19], in living water. But if you have not living water, baptize into other water; and if you can not in cold, in warm. But if you have not either, pour out water thrice upon the head into the name of Father and Son and Holy Spirit. But before the baptism let the baptizer fast, and the baptized, and whatever others can; but you shall order the baptized to fast one or two days before." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 7
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 7

topic: On the Ways of Light and Darkness
quote: "See that no one cause you to err from this way of the Teaching [i.e., the 'Way of Life'], since apart from God it teaches you. For if you are able to bear all the yoke of the Lord, you will be perfect; but if you are not able, what you are able that do." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 6
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 6

topic: On the Ways of Light and Darkness
quote: "And the way of death is this: First of all it is evil and full of curse: murders, adulteries, lusts, fornications, thefts, idolatries, magic arts, witchcrafts, rapines, false witnessings, hypocrisies, double-heartedness, deceit, haughtiness, depravity, self-will, greediness, filthy talking, jealousy, over-confidence, loftiness, boastfulness; persecutors of the good, hating truth, loving a lie, not knowing a reward for righteousness, not cleaving to good nor to righteous judgment, watching not for that which is good, but for that which is evil; from whom meekness and endurance are far, loving vanities, pursuing requital, not pitying a poor man, not laboring for the afflicted, not knowing Him that made them, murderers of children, destroyers of the handiwork of God, turning away from him that is in want, afflicting him that is distressed, advocates of the rich, lawless judges of the poor, utter sinners. Be delivered, children, from all these." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 5
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 5

quote: "The workings that befall you receive as good, knowing that apart from God nothing comes to pass." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 3
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 3

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "My child, flee from every evil thing, and from every likeness of it. Be not prone to anger, for anger leads the way to murder; neither jealous, nor quarrelsome, nor of hot temper; for out of all these murders are engendered. My child, be not a lustful one; for lust leads the way to fornication; neither a filthy talker, nor of lofty eye; for out of all these adulteries are engendered. My child, be not an observer of omens, since it leads the way to idolatry; neither an enchanter, nor an astrologer, nor a purifier, nor be willing to look at these things; for out of all these idolatry is engendered. My child, be not a liar, since a lie leads the way to theft; neither money-loving, nor vainglorious, for out of all these thefts are engendered. My child, be not a murmurer, since it leads the way to blasphemy; neither self-willed nor evil-minded, for out of all these blasphemies are engendered." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 3
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 3

topic: On the Ways of Light and Darkness
quote: "And the second commandment of the Teaching [i.e., of the 'Way of Life']; You shall not commit murder, you shall not commit adultery [Exodus 20:13-14], you shall not commit pederasty, you shall not commit fornication, you shall not steal [Exodus 20:15], you shall not practice magic, you shall not practice witchcraft, you shall not murder a child by abortion nor kill that which is begotten. You shall not covet the things of your neighbour [Exodus 20:17], you shall not forswear yourself [Matthew 5:34], you shall not bear false witness [Exodus 20:16], you shall not speak evil, you shall bear no grudge. You shall not be double-minded nor double-tongued; for to be double-tongued is a snare of death. Your speech shall not be false, nor empty, but fulfilled by deed. You shall not be covetous, nor rapacious, nor a hypocrite, nor evil disposed, nor haughty. You shall not take evil counsel against your neighbour. You shall not hate any man; but some you shall reprove, and concerning some you shall pray, and some you shall love more than your own life." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 2
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 2

quote: "In the church you shall acknowledge your transgressions, and you shall not come near for your prayer with an evil conscience." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 4
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 4

quote: "Forsake in no way the commandments of the Lord; but you shall keep what you have received, neither adding thereto nor taking away therefrom [Deuteronomy 12:32]." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 4
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 4

quote: "You shall not remove your hand from your son or from your daughter, but from their youth shall teach them the fear of God [Ephesians 6:4]." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 4
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 4

quote: "If you have anything, through your hands you shall give ransom for your sins. You shall not hesitate to give, nor murmur when you give; for you shall know who is the good repayer of the hire. You shall not turn away from him that is in want, but you shall share all things with your brother." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 4
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 4

quote: "Give to every one that asks you, and ask it not back; for the Father wills that to all should be given of our own blessings (free gifts). Happy is he that gives according to the commandment; for he is guiltless...But also now concerning this, it has been said, 'Let your alms sweat in your hands, until you know to whom you should give'." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 1
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 1

topic: On the Ways of Light and Darkness
quote: "And of these sayings the teaching is this: Bless those who curse you, and pray for your enemies, and fast for those who persecute you. For what reward is there, if you love those who love you? Do not also the Gentiles do the same? But love those who hate you, and you shall not have an enemy. Abstain from fleshly and worldly lusts. If someone gives you a blow upon your right cheek, turn to him the other also, and you shall be perfect. If someone impresses you for one mile, go with him two. If someone takes away your cloak, give him also your coat. If someone takes from you what is yours, ask it not back." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 1
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 1

topic: On the Ways of Light and Darkness
quote: "There are two ways, one of life and one of death; but a great difference between the two ways. The way of life, then, is this: First, you shall love God who made you; second, your neighbour as yourself; and all things whatsoever you would should not occur to you, do not also do to another." -- The Didache (c. 40-150 AD), The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 1
reference: The Didache (The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), Chapter 1

quote: "For our God, Jesus Christ, was, according to the appointment of God, conceived in the womb by Mary, of the seed of David, but by the Holy Ghost. He was born and baptized, that by His passion He might purify the water." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 18
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 18

quote: "For this end did the Lord allow the ointment to be poured upon His head [John 12:7], that He might breathe immortality into His Church. Be not anointed with the bad odor of the doctrine of the prince of this world; let him not lead you away captive from the life which is set before you." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 17
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 17

quote: "Do not err, my brethren [James 1:16]. Those that corrupt families shall not inherit the kingdom of God [1 Corinthians 6:9-10]. If, then, those who do this as respects the flesh have suffered death, how much more shall this be the case with any one who corrupts by wicked doctrine the faith of God, for which Jesus Christ was crucified! Such an one...shall go away into everlasting fire, and so shall every one that hearkens unto him." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 16
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 16

quote: "It is better for a man to be silent and be [a Christian], than to talk and not to be one...There is nothing which is hid from God, but our very secrets are near to Him." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 15
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 15

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "For the beginning is faith, and the end is love [1 Timothy 1:5]. Now these two, being inseparably connected together, are of God, while all other things which are requisite for a holy life follow after them. No man [truly] making a profession of faith sins [1 John 3:7]; nor does he that possesses love hate any one. The tree is made manifest by its fruit [Matthew 12:33]; so those that profess themselves to be Christians shall be recognized by their conduct. For there is not now a demand for mere profession, but that a man be found continuing in the power of faith to the end." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 14
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 14

quote: "And pray without ceasing on behalf of other men. For there is in them hope of repentance that they may attain to God. See, then, that they be instructed by your works, if in no other way. Be meek in response to their wrath, humble in opposition to their boasting: to their blasphemies return your prayers; in contrast to their error, be steadfast [Colossians 1:23] in the faith; and for their cruelty, manifest your gentleness. While we take care not to imitate their conduct, let us be found their brethren in all true kindness." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 10
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 10

quote: "There is one Physician who is possessed both of flesh and spirit; both made and not made; God existing in flesh; true life in death; both of Mary and of God; first passible and then impassible — even Jesus Christ our Lord." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 7
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 7

quote: "For some are in the habit of carrying about the name [of Jesus Christ] in wicked guile, while yet they practice things unworthy of God, whom you must flee as you would wild beasts. For they are ravening dogs, who bite secretly, against whom you must be on your guard, inasmuch as they are men who can scarcely be cured." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 7
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 7

quote: "Study, therefore, to be established in the doctrines of the Lord and the apostles, that so all things, whatsoever you do, may prosper both in the flesh and spirit; in faith and love; in the Son, and in the Father, and in the Spirit; in the beginning and in the end." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 13
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 13

quote: "For were He to reward us according to our works [i.e., that of the Mosaic Law], we should cease to be. Therefore, having become His disciples, let us learn to live according to the principles of Christianity...Lay aside, therefore, the evil, the old, the sour leaven, and be changed into the new leaven, which is Jesus Christ. Be salted in Him, lest any one among you should be corrupted, since by your savor you shall be convicted. It is absurd to profess Christ Jesus, and to Judaize. For Christianity did not embrace Judaism, but Judaism Christianity." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 10
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 10

quote: "Be not deceived with strange doctrines, nor with old fables, which are unprofitable. For if we still live according to the Jewish law, we acknowledge that we have not received grace. For the divinest prophets lived according to Christ Jesus. On this account also they were persecuted, being inspired by His grace to fully convince the unbelieving that there is one God, who has manifested Himself by Jesus Christ His Son, who is His eternal Word." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 8
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 8

quote: "Some that are without God, that is, the unbelieving, say, that He only seemed to suffer...Flee, therefore, those evil offshoots [of Satan], which produce death-bearing fruit, whereof if any one tastes, he instantly dies. For these men are not the planting of the Father." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapters 10-11
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapters 10-11

quote: "I therefore...entreat you that you use Christian nourishment only, and abstain from herbage of a different kind; I mean heresy. For those [that are given to this] mix up Jesus Christ with their own poison, speaking things which are unworthy of credit, like those who administer a deadly drug in sweet wine, which he who is ignorant of does greedily take, with a fatal pleasure leading to his own death." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 6
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 6

quote: "Am I not able to write to you of heavenly things? But I fear to do so, lest I should inflict injury on you who are but babes [in Christ]. Pardon me in this respect, lest, as not being able to receive [such doctrines], you should be strangled by them." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 5
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 5

quote: "Do not speak of Jesus Christ, and yet set your desires on the world." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, Chapter 7
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, Chapter 7

quote: "Let fire and the cross; let the crowds of wild beasts; let tearings, breakings, and dislocations of bones; let cutting off of members; let shatterings of the whole body; and let all the dreadful torments of the devil come upon me: only let me attain to Jesus Christ." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, Chapter 5
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, Chapter 5

quote: "For our God, Jesus Christ, now that He is with the Father, is all the more revealed [in His glory]." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, Chapter 3
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, Chapter 3

quote: "For where there is division and wrath, God does not dwell." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 8
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 8

quote: "But if any one preach the Jewish law unto you, listen not to him. For it is better to hearken to Christian doctrine from a man who has been circumcised, than to Judaism from one uncircumcised [i.e., Judaizers]." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 6
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 6

topic: On the Eucharist and Holy Communion
quote: "Take heed, then, to have but one Eucharist. For there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one cup to [show forth] the unity of His blood; one altar; as there is one bishop, along with the presbytery and deacons." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 4
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 4

quote: "Keep yourselves from those evil plants which Jesus Christ does not tend, because they are not the planting of the Father [i.e., heretics and schismatics]...For as many as are of God and of Jesus Christ are also with the bishop. And as many as shall, in the exercise of repentance, return into the unity of the Church, these, too, shall belong to God, that they may live according to Jesus Christ...If any man follows him that makes a schism in the Church, he shall not inherit the kingdom of God. If any one walks according to a strange opinion, he agrees not with the passion [of Christ]." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 3
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 3

topic: On the Eucharist and Holy Communion
quote: "Let that be deemed a proper Eucharist, which is [administered] either by the bishop, or by one to whom he has entrusted it." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 8
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 8

quote: "They abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, of His goodness, raised up again. Those, therefore, who speak against this gift of God, incur death in the midst of their disputes. But it were better for them to treat it with respect, that they also might rise again. It is fitting, therefore, that you should keep aloof from such persons, and not to speak of them either in private or in public." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 7
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 7

quote: "For what does any one profit me, if he commends me, but blasphemes my Lord, not confessing that He was [truly] possessed of a body? But he who does not acknowledge this, has in fact altogether denied Him, being enveloped in death." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 5
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 5

quote: "But I guard you beforehand from those beasts in the shape of men, whom you must not only not receive, but, if it be possible, not even meet with; only you must pray to God for them, if by any means they may be brought to repentance, which, however, will be very difficult." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 4
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 4

quote: "Now, He suffered all these things for our sakes, that we might be saved. And He suffered truly, even as also He truly raised up Himself, not, as certain unbelievers maintain, that He only seemed to suffer, as they themselves only seem to be [Christians]. And as they believe, so shall it happen unto them, when they shall be divested of their bodies, and be mere evil spirits." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 2
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 2

quote: "Let your works be the charge assigned to you, that you may receive a worthy recompense." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 6
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 6

quote: "Let your baptism endure as your arms; your faith as your helmet; your love as your spear; your patience as a complete panoply." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 6
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 6

quote: "Let none of you be found a deserter." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 6
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 6

quote: "Obey the bishop and the presbytery with an undivided mind, breaking one and the same bread [i.e., the Eucharist], which is the medicine of immortality, and the antidote to prevent us from dying, but [which causes] that we should live for ever in Jesus Christ." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 20
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 20

quote: "It is manifest, therefore, that we should look upon the bishop even as we would upon the Lord Himself." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 6
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 6

quote: "Let no man deceive himself: if any one be not within the altar, he is deprived of the bread of God. For if 'the prayer of one or two [Matthew 18:19]' possesses such power, how much more that of the bishop and the whole Church! He, therefore, that does not assemble with the Church, has even by this manifested his pride, and condemned himself...Let us be careful, then, not to set ourselves in opposition to the bishop, in order that we may be subject to God." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 5
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 5

quote: "Wherefore it is fitting that you should run together in accordance with the will of your bishop...For your justly renowned presbytery, worthy of God, is fitted as exactly to the bishop as the strings are to the harp. Therefore in your concord and harmonious love, Jesus Christ is sung." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 4
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 4

quote: "Being subject to the bishop and the presbytery, you may in all respects be sanctified." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 2
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 2

quote: "Being come together into the same place, let there be one prayer, one supplication, one mind, one hope, in love and in joy undefiled. There is one Jesus Christ, than whom nothing is more excellent. Therefore run together as into one temple of God, as to one altar, as to one Jesus Christ, who came forth from one Father, and is with and has gone to one." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 7
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 7

quote: "Be united with your bishop, and those that preside over you, as a type and evidence of your immortality." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 6
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 6

quote: "It is fitting, then, not only to be called Christians, but to be so in reality: as some indeed give one the title of bishop, but do all things without him. Now such persons seem to me to be not possessed of a good conscience, seeing they are not steadfastly gathered together according to the commandment." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 4
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians, Chapter 4

quote: "Continue in intimate union with Jesus Christ our God, and the bishop, and the enactments of the apostles...he who does anything apart from the bishop, and presbytery, and deacons, such a man is not pure in his conscience." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 7
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 7

quote: "In like manner, let all reverence the deacons as an appointment of Jesus Christ, and the bishop as Jesus Christ, who is the Son of the Father, and the presbyters as the sanhedrin of God, and assembly of the apostles. Apart from these, there is no Church." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 3
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 3

quote: "For, since you are subject to the bishop as to Jesus Christ, you appear to me to live not after the manner of men, but according to Jesus Christ, who died for us, in order, by believing in His death, you may escape from death. It is therefore necessary that, as you indeed do, so without the bishop you should do nothing, but should also be subject to the presbytery, as to the apostle of Jesus Christ, who is our hope, in whom, if we live, we shall [at last] be found. It is fitting also that the deacons, as being [the ministers] of the mysteries [i.e., Sacraments] of Jesus Christ, should in every respect be pleasing to all. For they are not ministers of meat and drink, but servants of the Church of God." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 2
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians, Chapter 2

quote: "To all them that repent, the Lord grants forgiveness, if they turn in penitence to the unity of God, and to communion with the bishop." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 8
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 8

quote: "Give heed to the bishop, and to the presbytery and deacons...Do nothing without the bishop." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 7
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 7

quote: "Wherefore, as children of light and truth, flee from division and wicked doctrines; but where the shepherd [i.e., the bishop] is, there follow as sheep." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 2
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians, Chapter 2

quote: "It is well to reverence both God and the bishop. He who honors the bishop has been honored by God; he who does anything without the knowledge of the bishop, does [in reality] serve the devil." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 9
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 9

quote: "Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church. It is not lawful without the bishop either to baptize or to celebrate a love-feast; but whatsoever he shall approve of, that is also pleasing to God, so that everything that is done may be secure and valid." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 8
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 8

quote: "See that you all follow the bishop, even as Jesus Christ does the Father, and the presbytery as you would the apostles; and reverence the deacons, as being the institution of God. Let no man do anything connected with the Church without the bishop." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 8
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, Chapter 8

quote: "Give heed to the bishop, that God also may give heed to you. My soul be for theirs that are submissive to the bishop, to the presbyters, and to the deacons, and may my portion be along with them in God!" -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 6
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 6

quote: "But it becomes both men and women who marry, to form their union with the approval of the bishop, that their marriage may be according to God, and not after their own lust." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 5
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 5

quote: "Give yourself to prayer without ceasing [1 Thessalonians 5:17]." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 1
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to Polycarp, Chapter 1

quote: "And this is despair, which cuts off from hope those who have been overthrown [i.e., by the devil]. This is the strong weapon of the enemy, and the only way in which he holds down those who have been made captives is by binding them with this chain, which, if we choose, we shall speedily be able to break by the grace of God." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 5
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 5

quote: "It is not possible for one who has departed to the other world to repent; no athlete, when he has quitted the lists, and the spectators have dispersed, can contend again." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 5
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 5

quote: "There is a resurrection, there is a judgment, there is a terrible tribunal which awaits us when we have gone out of this world; 'we must all stand before the judgment-seat of Christ [Romans 14:10]'. It is not in vain that we are threatened with hell fire, it is not without purpose that such great blessings have been prepared for us. The things of this life are a shadow, and more naught even than a shadow...Do not then deprive yourself both of that world, and of this, when you may gain both, if you please." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 5
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 5

quote: "Nothing is more precious than the soul; and even they who have gone to the extremity of folly have not been ignorant of this; 'for there is no equivalent of the soul' is the saying of a heathen poet [i.e., Saint John Chrysostom does not expand upon which Greek philosopher he had in mind]." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 3
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 3

quote: "For if he who has been attached to a heavenly bridegroom deserts him, and joins himself to a wife the act is adultery, even if you call it marriage ten thousand times over...what wonder is it if marriage condemns more than adultery when it involves the rejection of Christ?" -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 3
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 3

quote: "In that day each man will receive his due reward not according to the outward part which he has played [i.e., wealth, status, and power] but according to his works." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 3
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 3

quote: "And He will then sit as judge...What shall we say then...Or what defense shall we make, if we continue to disregard Him?...Shall we plead the anxieties of business?...Or that we have been deceived by others? But it did not help Adam in his defense to screen himself behind his wife, and say 'the woman whom you gave me, she deceived me [Genesis 3:12]'; even as the serpent was no excuse for the woman. Terrible...is that tribunal, one which needs no accusers and waits for no witnesses; for all things are naked and laid open to Him [Hebrews 4:13] who judges us, and we must submit to give an account not of deeds only but also of thoughts; for that judge is quick to discern the thoughts and intents of the heart [Hebrews 4:12]." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 2
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 2

quote: "There is nothing strange...in a wrestler falling, but in his remaining in a fallen condition; neither is it a grievous thing for the warrior to be wounded, but to despair after the blow has been struck, and to neglect the wound." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 1
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 1

quote: "You have blotted out your name from the list of the brethren, because you have trampled upon the covenant which you had made with Christ...For no one would indite a private individual for shunning military service; but when once a man has become a soldier, if he be caught deserting the ranks, he runs a risk of suffering the most extreme penalty." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 1
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 2, Section 1

quote: "For if the calamities of others are sufficient to instruct us, much more those which we have ourselves undergone...Only do not despair, do not fall back." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 19
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 19

quote: "If we do not store up in good time a measure of good deeds equivalent to the sins which are committed after them, nothing can hinder us from sinking grievously and completely...For he who departs to the other world with many deeds both good and bad, will have some alleviation in respect of the punishment and the torment there; but if a man is destitute of these good works, and takes only the evil with him, it is impossible to say what great sufferings he will undergo, when he is conducted to everlasting punishment. For a balance will be struck there between the evil deeds and those which are not such; and should the latter weigh down the scale they will to no small extent have saved the doer of them, and the injury arising from the doing of evil deeds is not so strong as to drag the man down from the foremost place; but if the evil deeds exceed, they carry him off into hell fire, because the number of his good actions is not so great as to be able to make a stand against this violent impulse. And these things are not merely suggested by our own reasoning, but declared also by the divine oracles; for He Himself says, 'He shall reward every man according to his works [Romans 2:6]'. And not only in hell, but also in the kingdom one will find many differences...'there is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon [1 Corinthians 15:41]'...He declares there is a difference in that world even between one star and another...let us never desist from doing good deeds, nor grow weary, nor, if we should be unable to reach the rank of the sun or of the moon, let us despise that of the stars. For if only we display thus much virtue at least, we shall be able to have a place in Heaven." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 19
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 19

quote: "And what is the root and mother of this despair? It is indolence; or rather one would not call it the root only, but also the nurse and mother. For as in the case of wool decay breeds moths...so here also indolence breeds despair, and is itself nourished in turn by despair; and thus supplying each other with this accursed exchange, they acquire no small additional power. If any one then cuts one of these off, and hews it in pieces, he will easily be able to get the better of the remaining one. For on the one hand he who is not indolent will never fall into despair, and on the other he who is supported by good hopes, and does not despair of himself, will not be able to fall into indolence. Pray then, wrench this pair asunder, and break the yoke in pieces." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 19
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 19

quote: "And what does spoil repentance is being again entangled in the same evils...Even so if a man fasts because of his sins, and goes his way again, and does the same things, who will hearken to his prayer? And again we read 'if a man goes back from righteousness to sin the Lord will prepare him for the sword [Sirach 26:28]'." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 18
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 18

quote: "It is possible for those who have come back again after repentance to shine with much luster, and oftentimes more than those who have never fallen at all." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 16
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 16

quote: "For the soul, when once it has abandoned its own salvation, will no longer perceive that it is plunging downwards, choosing to do and say everything which is adverse to its own salvation." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 16
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 16

quote: "Now if the confession of sins brings so much consolation, much more does the endeavor to wash them away by means of our deeds." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 15
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 15

topic: On the Ways of Light and Darkness
quote: "If...those who had once swerved from the straight path were forbidden to return to it again, perhaps no one, except a few persons...would ever enter the kingdom of Heaven." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 15
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 15

quote: "He then who is so anxious to be loved by us, and does everything for this end, and did not spare even His only begotten Son on account of His love towards us, and who counts it a desirable thing if at any time we become reconciled to Himself, how shall He not welcome and love us when we repent?" -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 15
reference: Two Exhortations to Theodore After His Fall, Letter 1, Section 15
