quote: "God the Father is neither begotten, nor proceeds from any other Person: the Son of God is from all eternity begotten of the Father: the Holy Spirit from all eternity proceeds from the Father." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, On the Articles of the Creed, On the First Article, Page 65
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, On the Articles of the Creed, On the First Article, Page 65

quote: "What is an Ecumenical Council? An assembly of the Pastors and Doctors of the catholic Church of Christ, as far as possible, from the whole world, for the confirmation of true doctrine and holy discipline among Christians." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, On Faith, Page 54
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, On Faith, Page 54

quote: "The most ancient and original instrument for spreading divine revelation is holy tradition. From Adam to Moses there were no sacred books. Our Lord Jesus Christ Himself delivered His divine doctrine and ordinances to His disciples by word and example, but not by writing. The same method was followed by the Apostles also at first, when they spread abroad the faith and established the Church of Christ. The necessity of tradition is further evident from this, that books can be available only to a small part of mankind, but tradition to all."  -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, On Holy Tradition and Holy Scripture, Page 37
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, On Holy Tradition and Holy Scripture, Page 37

quote: "By the name holy tradition is meant the doctrine of the faith, the law of God, the sacraments, and the ritual as handed down by the true believers and worshippers of God by word and example from one to another, and from generation to generation." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, On Holy Tradition and Holy Scripture, Page 36
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, On Holy Tradition and Holy Scripture, Page 36

quote: "What is necessary in order to please God and to save one's own soul? In the first place, a knowledge of the true God, and a right faith in Him; in the second place, a life according to faith, and good works." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, Introduction to the Longer Catechism, Page 29
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Longer Catechism, Introduction to the Longer Catechism, Page 29

quote: "Let us eagerly run our course as men called by our God and King, lest, since our time is short, we be found in the day of our death without fruit and perish of hunger." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 1, Section 15
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 1, Section 15
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "The past wounds therefore of soul and body God heals by Baptism; against future ones let us one and all jointly guard ourselves, that we may keep this vestment of the body pure, and may not for practising fornication and sensual indulgence or any other sin for a short season, lose the salvation of heaven, but may inherit the eternal kingdom of God; of which may God, of His own grace, deem all of you worthy." -- Saint Cyril of Jerusalem (313-386 AD), Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 18, Section 20
reference: Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 18, Section 20

quote: "But let not Christ be forsaken, so that the loss of salvation and of an eternal home should be feared." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 3, Section 10
reference: Treatises, Treatise 3, Section 10

quote: "We ought...ourselves to fear, lest perchance, after [we have come to] the knowledge of Christ, if we do things displeasing to God, we obtain no further forgiveness of sins, but be shut out from His kingdom." -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Against Heresies, Book 4, Chapter 27, Section 2
reference: Against Heresies, Book 4, Chapter 27, Section 2

quote: "Those, on the other hand, who depart from Him, and despise His precepts, and by their deeds bring dishonour on Him who made them, and by their opinions blaspheme Him who nourishes them, heap up against themselves most righteous judgment." -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Against Heresies, Book 4, Chapter 33, Section 15
reference: Against Heresies, Book 4, Chapter 33, Section 15

quote: "The Lord thus making it manifest that He does not forsake those that hope in Him, but gives up such as depart from Him to punishment and torture." -- Saint Clement of Rome (35-100 AD), The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, Chapter 11, Section 1
reference: The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, Chapter 11, Section 1

topic: On the Ways of Light and Darkness
quote: "The way of light, then, is as follows. If any one desires to travel to the appointed place, he must be zealous in his works." -- Saint Barnabas (died ~61 AD), The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter 19
reference: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter 19

quote: "The tree is made manifest by its fruit; so those that profess themselves to be Christians shall be recognised by their conduct. For there is not now a demand for mere profession, but that a man be found continuing in the power of faith to the end." -- Saint Ignatius of Antioch (35-107 AD), The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 14, Paragraph 1
reference: The Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, Chapter 14, Paragraph 1

quote: "But he follows Christ who stands in His precepts, who walks in the way of His teaching, who follows His footsteps and His ways, who imitates that which Christ both did and taught...To put on the name of Christ, and not to go in the way of Christ, what else is it but a mockery of the divine name, but a desertion of the way of salvation; since He Himself teaches and says that he shall come unto life who keeps His commandments." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 10, Sections 11-12
reference: Treatises, Treatise 10, Sections 11-12

quote: "We have an advocate and an intercessor for our sins, Jesus Christ the Lord and our God, if only we repent of our sins past, and confess and acknowledge our sins, whereby we now offend the Lord, and for the time to come engage to walk in His ways, and to fear His commandments." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 7, Section 5
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 7, Section 5

quote: "Icons, that is, representations of the true God in the flesh, and of His Saints, are rightly used for the religious remembrance of the works of God, and of His Saints, and it is right to pray before them to God and to His Saints. Nevertheless, this right and godly honor of Icons may be abused so as to become the sin of idolatry, if anyone honors only the holy Icons themselves, and trusts in their material substance, without raising up his mind and heart to Christ and His Saints whom they represent." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Of the Ten Commandments, Page 22
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Of the Ten Commandments, Page 22

quote: "But what if we do not forgive others? Then we can expect no forgiveness ourselves of God; and so it is absolutely necessary to forgive injuries, and strive to be at peace with all men." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Of the Lord's Prayer, Page 20
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Of the Lord's Prayer, Page 20

quote: "After the general resurrection and Christ's judgment there shall be an everlasting life, in which believers, who have ended their course on earth in repentance and good works, shall receive everlasting bliss; but impenitent sinners shall suffer everlasting torment." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Of the Creed, Pages 16-17
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Of the Creed, Pages 16-17

quote: "The true Christian Church is one, holy, catholic or ecumenical, and Apostolic, that is, derived from the Apostles to us without break or change, and so to be continued to the end of the world: and therefore it is our duty to reverence her, and obey her, and flee all schism; that is, separation from the one Orthodox Church." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Of the Creed, Page 14
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Of the Creed, Page 14

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "Whence may we best learn how to believe aright? From the Creed." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Introduction to the Shorter Catechism, Page 9
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Introduction to the Shorter Catechism, Page 9

quote: "How can we draw near to God? By thought, desire, and deed. Who draws near to God by thought? He who rightly believes in Him. Who draws near to God by desire? He who prays to Him. Who draws near to God by deed? He who walks after God's will and law." -- Saint Philaret of Moscow (1782-1867 AD), The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Introduction to the Shorter Catechism, Page 9
reference: The Longer Catechism of the Eastern Orthodox Church, The Shorter Catechism, Introduction to the Shorter Catechism, Page 9

quote: "How can a man say that he believes in Christ, if he does not do what Christ commanded him to do? From where will he attain the reward of faith, if he will not keep the faith of the commandment? He will make no advancement in his walk toward salvation, for he does not keep the truth of the way of salvation." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 1, Section 2
reference: Treatises, Treatise 1, Section 2

quote: "With respect to obedience and doctrine, we are not all the sons of God. Rather, it is only those who truly believe in Him and do His will. Now, those who do not believe, and do not obey His will, are sons and angels of the devil...Those who do not obey Him, being disinherited by Him, have ceased to be His sons." -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Against Heresies, Book 4, Chapter 41, Section 2
reference: Against Heresies, Book 4, Chapter 41, Section 2

quote: "It is good therefore to learn the ordinances of the Lord, as many as have been written above, and to walk in them. For he that does these things shall be glorified in the kingdom of God; whereas he that chooses their opposites shall perish together with his works. For this cause is the resurrection, for this the recompense." -- Saint Barnabas (died ~61 AD), The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter 21
reference: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter 21

quote: "Christ demands not the doing of the commandments, but the soul's amendment, because of which He gave His commandments to rational beings." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 57, Page 282
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 57, Page 282

quote: "And let those who are not found living as He taught, be understood to be no Christians, even though they profess with the lip the precepts of Christ; for not those who make profession, but those who do the works, shall be saved, according to His word: 'Not everyone who saith to Me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he that doeth the will of my Father, which is in heaven [Matthew 7:21]'." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 16
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 16

quote: "But how can we possess immortality, unless we keep those commands of Christ whereby death is driven out and overcome, when He Himself warns us, and says, 'If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments [Matthew 19:17]’?" -- Saint Cyprian (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 1, Section 2
reference: Treatises, Treatise 1, Section 2

quote: "We need to be careful not to harbor any resentment against those who harm us, but rather to pray for them with love. Whatever any of our fellow men does, we should never think evil of him. We need to always have thoughts of love and always to think good of others." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Dispositions of the Heart, Page 212
reference: Wounded By Love, On Dispositions of the Heart, Page 212

quote: "Be a true Christian. Then you won't leap to conclusions about anybody, but your love will 'cover all things [1 Cor. 13:7].' Even to a person of another religion you will always act as a Christian. That is to say, you will show respect for him in a gracious manner irrespective of his religion. You will care for a Muslim when he is in need, speak to him, and keep company with him. There must be respect for the freedom of the other person. Just as Christ 'stands at the door and knocks [Rev. 3:20]' and does not force an entry, but waits for the soul to accept him freely on its own, so we should stand in the same way in relation to every soul." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Love For One's Neighbor, Page 187
reference: Wounded By Love, On Love For One's Neighbor, Page 187

quote: "We shouldn't be enraged by people who blaspheme or who speak and act against God and the Church. Such rage is harmful. We may hate the words and the malice behind them, but we must not hate the person who spoke them nor become enraged against him. Rather we should pray for him. A Christian has love and graciousness and should behave accordingly." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Love For One's Neighbor, Page 184
reference: Wounded By Love, On Love For One's Neighbor, Page 184

quote: "God has placed a power in man's soul. But it is up to him how he channels it--for good or for evil. If we imagine the good as a garden full of flowers, trees, and plants and the evil as weeds and thorns and the power as water, then what can happen is as follows: when the water is directed towards the flower-garden, then all the plants grow, blossom, and bear fruit; and at the same time, the weeds and thorns, because they are not being watered, wither and die. And the opposite, of course, can also happen. It is not necessary therefore to concern yourselves with the weeds. Don't occupy yourself with rooting out evil. Christ does not wish us to occupy ourselves with the passions, but with the opposite. Channel the water, that is, all the strength of your soul, to the flowers and you will enjoy their beauty, their fragrance, and their freshness. You won't become saints by hounding after evil. Ignore evil. Look towards Christ, and He will save you." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 135
reference: Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 135

quote: "When abused, you bless; when slandered, you praise; and when tricked, you make maintain your affection. This is the way of Christ's philosophy: if you do not follow it, you do not share His company." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (580-662 AD), Philokalia (Vol. I), Four Hundred Texts on Love, Fourth Century, Section 30
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), Four Hundred Texts on Love, Fourth Century, Section 30

quote: "Let us pay close attention to ourselves so that we are not deceived into thinking that we are following the straight and narrow way when in actual fact we are keeping to the wide and broad way. The following will show you what the narrow way means: mortification of the stomach, all night standing, water in moderation, short rations of bread, the purifying draught of dishonor, sneers derision, insults, the cutting out of one's own will, patience in annoyances, unmurmering endurance of scorn, disregard of insults, and the habit, when wronged, of bearing it sturdily; when slandered, of not being indignant; when humiliated, not to be angry; when condemned, to be humble. Blessed are they who follow the way we have just described, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 2, Section 8
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 2, Section 8
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "For to follow the Savior is to be a partaker of salvation, and to follow light is to receive light. But those who are in light do not themselves illumine the light, but are illumined and revealed by it: they do certainly contribute nothing to it, but, receiving the benefit, they are illumined by the light." -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Against Heresies, Book 4, Chapter 14, Paragraph 1
reference: Against Heresies, Book 4, Chapter 14, Paragraph 1

quote: "Each man goes to everlasting punishment or salvation according to the value of his actions. For if all men knew this, no one would choose wickedness even for a little, knowing that he goes to the everlasting punishment of fire; but would by all means restrain himself, and adorn himself with virtue, that he might obtain the good gifts of God and escape the punishments." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), First Apology, Chapter 12
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 12

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "You don't become holy by fighting evil. Let evil be. Look towards Christ and that will save you. What makes a person saintly is love." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 156
reference: Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 156

quote: "Attention must be concentrated principally on carrying out the commandments. We already believe, what else is needed? Carry out the commandments, for 'faith without works is dead [James 2:20]'." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 17, Page 92
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 17, Page 92

quote: "The great secret to rid yourself of depression and all that is negative is to give yourself over to the love of God. Something that can help a person who is depressed is work, interest in life, the garden, plants, flowers, trees, the countryside, a walk in the open air; all these things lift a person out of inactivity and awaken other interests. They they act like medicines. To occupy oneself with the arts, with music, and so on, is very beneficial. The thing that I place at the top of the list, however, is interest in the Church, in reading the Holy Scriptures, and in attending services." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Page 179
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Page 179

quote: "This state [i.e., depression] is cured by grace. The soul must turn to God's love and the cure will come when we start to love God passionately. Many of our Saints transformed depression into joy through their love for Christ. They took this power of the soul which the devil wished to crush, gave it to God, and transformed it into joy and exaltation, prayer, and worship." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Pages 178-179
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Pages 178-179

quote: "Take heed, lest resting at our ease, as those who are the called, we fall asleep in our sins. For then, the wicked prince, acquiring power over us, will thrust us away from the kingdom of the Lord." -- Saint Barnabas (died ~61 AD), The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter 4
reference: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter 4

quote: "We ought therefore, brethren, carefully to inquire concerning our salvation. Otherwise, the wicked one, having made his entrance by deceit, may hurl us forth from our life." -- Saint Barnabas (died ~61 AD), The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter 2
reference: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter 2

quote: "So then before looking at the sun, which is humility, we must be illumined by the light, which is meekness, and then we can look with a clear gaze at the sun." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 24, Section 1
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 24, Section 1
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Meekness is the fellow-worker of obedience, the guide of the brotherhood, a curb for the furious, a check to the irritable, a minister of joy, the imitation of Christ, something proper to angels, shackles for demons, a shield against peevishness." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 24, Section 6
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 24, Section 6
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "For God is manifested not in labors but in simplicity and humility. And if the power of the Lord is made perfect in weakness, the Lord will certainly not reject a humble worker." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 52
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 52
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "If the pride of some of the angels made them demons, no doubt humility can make angels out of demons. So those who have fallen may take courage!" -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 63
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 63
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "We should unceasingly condemn and reproach ourselves so as to cast off involuntary sins through voluntary humiliations. Otherwise, if we do not, at our departure we shall certainly be subjected to heavy punishment." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 55
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 55
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "He who has taken humility as his bride is above all gentle, kind, full of compunction, sympathetic, calm, bright, compliant, inoffensive, wide awake, not indolent and (why say more?) free from passion; for the Lord remembered us in our humility, and delivered us from our enemies, and our passions and impurities." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 10
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 10
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "An angel fell from heaven without any other passion except pride, and so we may ask whether it is possible to ascend to heaven by humility alone without any other of the virtues." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 12
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 12
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "I have seen how in the world they planted many different plants of the virtues, which were watered by vainglory as by an underground sewage pipe, and were hoed by ostentation, and for manure were heaped with praise. But when transplanted to a desert soil...they withered at once." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 2, Section 6
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 2, Section 6
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Humility, even without works, gains forgiveness for many offenses; but without her, works are of no profit to us, and rather prepare for us great evils." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 69, Page 338
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 69, Page 338

quote: "No man has understanding if he is not humble, and he who lacks humility is devoid of understanding. No man is humble if he is not peaceful, and he who is not peaceful is not humble." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Acetical Homilies, Homily 51, Page 247
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 51, Page 247

quote: "'But,' you may well ask, 'what means are there of acquiring humility?' Well, we acquire this art through reading the Fathers; pitiless self-examination and self-accusation help too; also, making clear to ourselves how much worse we are than others; and refraining from all condemnation of them while we accept all their condemnation of us, as sent by God to cure our hideous spiritual sores." -- Saint Macarius of Optina (1788-1860), Letters of Elder Macarius of Optina, Blessed Are the Pure in Heart: For They Shall See God, Chapter 4, Paragraph 3
reference: Letters of Elder Macarius of Optina, Blessed Are the Pure in Heart: For They Shall See God, Chapter 4, Paragraph 3

quote: "Fear of God, love, and humility are the medicine [i.e., for anger]. Pride is the root of this besetting passion of yours." -- Saint Macarius of Optina (1788-1860), Letters of Elder Macarius of Optina, Blessed Are the Pure in Heart: For They Shall See God, Chapter 2, Paragraph 1
reference: Letters of Elder Macarius of Optina, Blessed Are the Pure in Heart: For They Shall See God, Chapter 2, Paragraph 1

quote: "It is infinitely better for us to see ourselves as bad than good. In the first case, we acquire humility, and find the door to forgiveness, the door to grace; in the second, we grow proud; and pride blocks the way to grace." -- Saint Macarius of Optina (1788-1860), Letters of Elder Macarius of Optina, Blessed Are the Poor in Spirit: For Theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven, Chapter 2, Paragraph 1
reference: Letters of Elder Macarius of Optina, Blessed Are the Poor in Spirit: For Theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven, Chapter 2, Paragraph 1

quote: "Resurrection is the restoration of our nature to its original condition. In the first life, of which God Himself became the creator, there was presumably neither old age, nor infancy, nor the sufferings caused by the many kinds of diseases, nor any other type of bodily misery; for it is not likely that God created such things. Human nature was a divine sort of thing, before humanity started on the course of evil. All these things attacked us when evil entered our life." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 10, Page 113
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 10, Page 113
tags: God is not the author of evil

quote: "If such distinctions were made in this Temple [i.e., the outer walls, the veil, the sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, etc.], which was a kind of image and copy of the spiritual condition, the physical observance teaches us that not all rational beings approach the Temple of God (that is the confession of the great God), but those who have strayed the false beliefs are outside the divine enclosure. Moreover, among those who have come inside by the strength of their confession, those who have cleansed themselves in advance by purifications and chastity are honored more than the others; and among these, those who have dedicated themselves to the ascetic life already have the greater part, so that they are counted worthy to enter into the inner mysteries." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 10, Pages 105-106
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 10, Pages 105-106

quote: "He is saying [i.e., David in Psalm 103(104):29-30] that the power of the Spirit, accomplishing everything in everything, both gives life to those whom it enters and removes from life those from whom it departs. He says that the death of the living happens by the departure of the Spirit, and by Its presence the renewal of the dead takes place. Because the death of those who are being renewed comes first in the order of the words, we can say that the mystery of the resurrection is being proclaimed to the Church, as David has foretold this grace by his spirit of prophecy." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 10, Page 104
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 10, Page 104

quote: "Virtue has no master. Therefore, everything free will be in virtue, for that which is free also has no master. But indeed the divine Nature is the source of all virtue. Hence those who are released from evil will be in the divine Nature, so that, as the apostle says, 'God may be all in all [1 Corinthians 15:28]'." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Page 86
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Page 86

quote: "The just judgment of God pursues all and adjusts the necessary recompense to equal the gravity of the debt, without overlooking even the least. The Gospel says that the restitution for the debt is not made by payment of money, but that the debtor is handed over 'to the torturers until,' it says, 'he pays back all that he owes [Matthew 18:34]'. This means simply that by the torment he pays the necessary obligation, the debt of participation in distress which incurred during his life by foolishly choosing pleasure straight and unmixed with its opposite. When he has thus put away all that is alien to him (which is sin) and taken off the shameful garment of his debts, he enters into freedom and confidence." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Pages 85-86
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Pages 85-86

quote: "For evil must be altogether removed in every way from being, and, as we have said before, that which does not really exist must cease to exist at all. Since evil does not exist by its nature outside of free choice, when all choice is in God, evil will suffer a complete annihilation because no receptacle remains for it." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Page 85
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Page 85
tags: God is not the author of evil

quote: "When goldsmiths purify gold by fire from the matter which is mixed with it, they do not only melt the adulterant in the fire, but inevitably the pure metal is melted along with the base admixture. When the latter is consumed, the former remains. In the same way when evil is consumed by the purifying fire, the soul which is united to evil must necessarily also be in the fire until the base adulterant material is removed, consumed by the fire...Something like this I think we should imagine for the state of the soul. Wrapped up as it is in material and earthly attachments, it struggles and is stretched, as God draws His own to Himself. What is alien to God has to be scraped off forcibly because it has somehow grown onto the soul. This is the cause of the sharp and unbearable pains which the soul must endure [i.e., in being purified]." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Page 84
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Page 84

quote: "For it is not out of hatred or vengeance for an evil life (in my opinion) that God brings painful conditions upon sinners...but for a better purpose He draws the soul to Himself, Who is the fountain of all blessedness." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Page 83
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 7, Page 83

quote: "All the evil feelings such as insecurity, despair, and disenchantment that come to take control of the soul disappear with humility." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Page 178
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Page 178

quote: "With humility you attract the grace of God. You surrender yourself to the love of God, to worship, and to prayer. But even if you do all in the world you achieve nothing if you haven't acquired humility." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Page 178
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Page 178

quote: "This is what he [i.e., Saint Hesychius] says: 'One who is engaged in the spiritual struggle must have at every moment the following four things: humility, extreme attentiveness, refutation (of the thoughts) and prayer'." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How To Be Attuned to It, Chapter 59, Page 250
reference: The Spiritual Life and How To Be Attuned to It, Chapter 59, Page 250

quote: "Concern yourself with your own sins and not with those of your neighbor; then the workplace of your intellect will not be robbed." -- Saint Mark the Ascetic (died 430 AD), Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Spiritual Law: Two Hundred Texts, Section 63
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Spiritual Law: Two Hundred Texts, Section 63

quote: "Where there is no light, everything is dark; where there is no humility, all that we have is rotten." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 16
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 16
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "In proportion to your humility you are given patience in your woes; and in proportion to your patience the burden of your afflictions is made lighter and you will find consolation; in proportion to your consolation, your love of God increases; and in proportion to your love, your joy in the Holy Spirit is magnified." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 42, Page 212
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 42, Page 212

quote: "A horse when alone often imagines that it is galloping, but when it is with others it finds out how slow it is." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 21
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 21
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "In drawing water from a well we sometimes without noticing it bring up a frog with the water, and so in acquiring the virtues we often get involved in the vices that are imperceptibly entwined with them. The kind of thing I mean is that gluttony is entangled with hospitality; lust with love; cunning with discernment...and behind them all as a general salve, or rather poison, follows vainglory." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 58
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 58
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Repentance raises the fallen, mourning knocks at the gate of heaven, and holy humility opens it." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 15
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 25, Section 15
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "The Lord seems to be teaching [i.e., in the Parable of the Rich man and Lazarus] that we who are living in the flesh ought as much as possible to separate ourselves and release ourselves from its hold by the life of virtue, so that after death we may not need another death to cleanse us from the remains of the fleshly glue. Then, as if chains have been broken away from the soul, its course may become light and easy towards the good, when no bodily weight drags the soul to itself." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 6, Pages 75-76
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 6, Pages 75-76

quote: "So if one should become completely carnal in his mind, devoting all the activity and energy of his soul to the will of the flesh, such a man even when he gets out of the flesh is not separated from its experiences. Those who spend most of their time and evil-smelling places, even if they go out into the fresh air, are not cleansed from the unpleasantness which has adhered to them from prolonged contact. In the same way, even when the transition has been made to the invisible and rarified life [i.e., when they have died], the lovers of the flesh would doubtless be unable to avoid bringing with them some of the fleshly odor." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 6, Page 76
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 6, Page 76

quote: "There seems to be some support for this opinion in what certain people say, that often around the bodies' graves there appear some kind of shadowy shapes of the departed. If this really happens, it proves that the soul has become more attached than it should be to the present fleshly life, so that even when it is driven out of the flesh it is not willing to fly clean away." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 6, Page 76
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 6, Page 76

quote: "It is likely that this Hades...is not intended to signify a place with that name. The Scripture must be teaching us that it is some invisible and incorporeal condition of life, in which the soul lives." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 5, Page 73
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 5, Page 73

quote: "The divine Providence gave us power because of His love for mankind to have each of these (I mean the good and the evil) in whichever we wish, either in this short and transient life or in those endless ages whose limit is infinity." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 5, Page 71
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 5, Page 71

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "That which alone is truly good by nature [i.e., passions intended for virtue] has also been overshadowed by the plant of deceit growing up along with it [i.e., passions used for evil]. For the desiring faculty has grown and matured not towards the good by nature, for the sake of which it was sown in us, but instead it has made the harvest beastly and irrational...In the same way also the seed of anger has not been tempered into courage, but has armed us for battle with our own kind. Likewise the power of love has turned away from the intelligible, running riot in the immoderate enjoyment of the sensual. The other emotions in the same way have produced the worse plants instead of the better. For this reason the wise farmer allows the plant which has grown in with the seed to remain with it, taking care that we may not be deprived of the better part, as we might be if desire were altogether rooted out along with the useless growth. For if this should happen to our human nature, what is there which would raise us towards the union with the heavenly? Or if love is taken away, in what manner will we be joined with the divine? If anger is quenched, what weapon will we have against our adversary? So you see the farmer leaves the bastard seeds in us, intending not that they should permanently dominate the more honorable sowing, but that the field itself (for so he figuratively names the heart) through the natural power residing in it (which is reason), should dry up one part of the plants, but render the other part fruitful and thriving. But if this does not happen, he assigns to the fire the task of sorting out the harvest." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 59
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 59

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "But if instead the passions rule over the power of the mind, our humanity is changed from intelligence and godlikeness to irrationality and mindlessness. We are turned into beasts by the force of these passions." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 58
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 58

quote: "But as our conflicts increase, so do our crowns. He who has never been struck by the enemy will certainly not be crowned. But the warrior who does not flinch despite his incidental falls will be glorified by the angels as a champion." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 157
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 157
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Since to those who have done well shall be assigned righteously eternal bliss, and to the lovers of iniquity shall be given eternal punishment. And the fire which is un-quenchable and without end awaits these latter, and a certain fiery worm which dies not, and which does not waste the body, but continues bursting forth from the body with unending pain. No sleep will give them rest; no night will soothe them; no death will deliver them from punishment; no voice of interceding friends will profit them." -- Saint Hippolytus of Rome (170-235 AD), Against Plato, On the Cause of the Universe, Section 3
reference: Against Plato, On the Cause of the Universe, Section 3

quote: "'Until the Ancient of days come [Daniel 7:22]'. That is, when at length the Judge of judges and the King of kings comes from heaven, who shall subvert the whole dominion and power of the adversary, and shall consume all with the eternal fire of punishment. But to His servants, and prophets, and martyrs, and to all who fear Him, He will give an everlasting kingdom; that is, they shall possess the endless enjoyment of good." -- Saint Hippolytus of Rome (170-235 AD), Fragments from the Scriptural Commentaries of Hippolytus, On Daniel, Third fragment (Scholia on Daniel), Section 22
reference: Fragments from the Scriptural Commentaries of Hippolytus, On Daniel, Third fragment (Scholia on Daniel), Section 22

quote: "But the souls of the unrighteous meet an untimely expulsion from the presence of God, by whom they shall be left to remain in the flame of torment." -- Saint Hippolytus of Rome (170-235 AD), Fragments from the Scriptural Commentaries of Hippolytus, On Proverbs, First Fragment
reference: Fragments from the Scriptural Commentaries of Hippolytus, On Proverbs, First Fragment

quote: "The advent of the Son comes indeed alike to all, but is for the purpose of judging, and separating the believing from the unbelieving, since, as those who believe do His will agreeably to their own choice, and as, [also] agreeably to their own choice, the disobedient do not consent to His doctrine; it is manifest that His Father has made all in a like condition, each person having a choice of his own, and a free understanding." -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Against Heresies, Book 5, Chapter 27, Section 1
reference: Against Heresies, Book 5, Chapter 27, Section 1

quote: "'We must all appear at the judgment-seat of Christ, and must every one give an account of himself [Romans 14:10-12 and 2 Corinthians 5:10].' Let us then serve Him in fear and with all reverence, even as He Himself has commanded us, and as the apostles who preached the Gospel unto us, and the prophets who proclaimed beforehand the coming of the Lord [have alike taught us]." -- Saint Polycarp (69-155 AD), Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians, Chapter 6
reference: Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians, Chapter 6

quote: "How then, some one will say, are we to escape the fire? And how to enter into the kingdom? 'I was an hungered,' He says, 'and you gave Me meat.' Learn hence the way; there is here no need of allegory, but to fulfil what is said. 'I was an hungered, and you gave Me meat; I was thirsty, and you gave Me drink; I was a stranger, and you took Me in; naked, and you clothed Me; I was sick, and you visited Me; I was in prison, and you came unto Me.' These things if you do, you shall reign together with Him; but if you do them not, you shall be condemned. At once then begin to do these works, and abide in the faith; lest, like the foolish virgins, tarrying to buy oil, thou be shut out. Be not confident because thou merely possessest the lamp, but constantly keep it burning." -- Saint Cyril of Jerusalem (313-386 AD), Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 15, Section 26
reference: Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 15, Section 26
tags: exclusion from the kingdom of Heaven

quote: "When the servant does not do what is commanded, the Lord will do what He threatens...'I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat. I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink...and these will go away into everlasting burning: but the righteous into life eternal.' What more could Christ declare unto us? How more could He stimulate the works of our righteousness and mercy, than by saying that whatever is given to the needy and poor is given to Himself, and by saying that He is aggrieved unless the needy and poor be supplied?" -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 8, Section 23
reference: Treatises, Treatise 8, Section 23

quote: "When the day of judgment shall come, what joy of believers, what sorrow of unbelievers; that they should have been unwilling to believe here, and now that they should be unable to return that they might believe! An ever-burning Gehenna will burn up the condemned, and a punishment devouring with living flames; nor will there be any source whence at any time they may have either respite or end to their torments. Souls with their bodies will be reserved in infinite tortures for suffering." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 5, Section 24
reference: Treatises, Treatise 5, Section 24

quote: "Oh, what and how great will that day be at its coming, beloved brethren, when the Lord shall begin to count up His people, and to recognize the deservings of each one by the inspection of His divine knowledge, to send the guilty to Gehenna, and to set on fire our persecutors with the perpetual burning of a penal fire, but to pay to us the reward of our faith and devotion!'" -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 55, Section 10
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 55, Section 10

quote: "Do not be self-confident until you hear the final sentence passed upon yourself, bearing in mind the guest who got as far as to joining in the marriage feast and then was bound hand and foot and cast out into outer darkness [i.,e., Matthew 22:13]." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), Step 23, Section 17
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 17
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Every man will suffer punishment in eternal fire according to the merit of his deed, and will render account according to the power he has received from God [Luke 12:48]." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), The First Apology, Chapter 17
reference: The First Apology, Chapter 17

quote: "When you come to say in your heart 'I am guilty,' then you must apply the fear of the Divine Judgment. If your own conscience condemns you, then God Himself does not excuse you. And God does see you as guilty. If you are seen as such, then you are condemned as such." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 36, Pages 164-165
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 36, Pages 164-165

quote: "A gracious God gives us the hope of forgiveness of guilt, if we repent with contrition and set forth a firm intention to flee past sins and not anger God by them. This is the essence of repentance." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 36, Page 165
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 36, Page 165

quote: "Fix in your mind the remembrance that God is everywhere, both outside you and within, and never be separated from this remembrance as you go about; work, sit, sleep and be awake with it. Join to this another remembrance, that of death, and that upon death, there will be the judgment and determination of eternal fate. These two remembrances are the two powerful guards of everything good. They themselves will teach you everything, kindling inside you the saving fear of God, the source of divine wisdom." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 72, Page 292
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 72, Page 292

quote: "May the fear of death and of the judgment at death never leave you. From morning, at the same time you are renewing the memory of the Lord in your heart, take care to add to this memory of these final things...You will see what safeguards these are." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 46, Page 202
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 46, Page 202

quote: "Hasty and severe judges of the sins of their neighbor fall into this predicament [i.e., inevitably being judged for the same sins they are judging others for] because they have not yet attained to a thorough and constant remembrance and concern for their own sins. For if anyone could see his own vices accurately without the veil of self-love, he would worry about nothing else in this life, considering that he would not have time enough for mourning for himself even though he were to live a hundred years, and even though he were to see a whole river Jordan of tears streaming from his eyes." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 10
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 10
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Do not cease to picture and scrutinize the dark abyss of eternal fire, and the merciless servants, the unsympathetic and in exorable Judge, the bottomless pit of subterranean flame, the narrow descents to the awful underground chambers and yawning gulfs, and all such things, so that the sensuality in our soul may be checked by great terror and give place to incorruptible chastity, and itself receive the shining of the immaterial light which radiates beyond any fire." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 7, Section 10
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 7, Section 10
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "He who has mounted [i.e., the remembrance of death] will never sin again. ‘Remember thy last end and thou shalt never sin [Ecclesiasticus 7:36]’." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 6, Section 24
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 6, Section 24
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "It is impossible...to spend the present day devoutly unless we regard it as the last of our whole life." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 6, Section 24
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 6, Section 24
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Acquire an inseparable wife--the remembrance of death. And let your beloved children be the sighs of your heart. Make your body your slave; and your friends, the Holy Powers (Angels) who can help you at the hour of your death, if they become your friends. This is the generation (family) of those who seek the Lord." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 3, Section 15
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 3, Section 15
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Now, any substance, when brought in contact with what is of a similar nature, will not be dissolved into nothing, nor will be in danger of perishing, but will rather continue and increase, such as fire in fire, spirit in spirit, and water in water; but those which are of a contrary nature to each other do, [when they meet,] suffer and are changed and destroyed [i.e., refuting how Gnostics teach that incorruption results in corruption with spiritual beings; a common Gnostic teaching]." -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Against Heresies, Book 2, Chapter 18, Paragraph 5
reference: Against Heresies, Book 2, Chapter 18, Paragraph 5

quote: "And, therefore, God invented death for our sakes, that He might destroy sin, lest rising up in us immortals, as I said, it should be immortal." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (250-311 AD), From the Discourse on the Resurrection, Part 3, A Synopsis of Some Apostolic Words from the Same Discourse, Paragraph 2
reference: From the Discourse on the Resurrection, Part 3, A Synopsis of Some Apostolic Words from the Same Discourse, Paragraph 2

quote: "Since it was for this reason that death was appointed by God for the sinner, that evil might not remain forever." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (250-311 AD), From the Discourse on the Resurrection, Part 3, Paragraph 10
reference: From the Discourse on the Resurrection, Part 3, Paragraph 10

quote: "For no one can boast of being so free from sin as not even to have an evil thought." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (250-311 AD), From the Discourse on the Resurrection, Part 1, Paragraph 5
reference: From the Discourse on the Resurrection, Part 1, Paragraph 5

quote: "For while the body still lives, before it has passed through death, sin must also live with it, as it has its roots concealed within us even though it be externally checked by the wounds inflicted by corrections and warnings; since, otherwise, it would not happen that we do wrong after baptism, as we should be entirely and absolutely free from sin." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (250-311 AD), From the Discourse on the Resurrection, Part 1, Paragraph 5
reference: From the Discourse on the Resurrection, Part 1, Paragraph 5

quote: "God putting an end to sin by means of death, lest man immortal, living a sinner, and sin living in him, should be liable to eternal curse. Wherefore he died, although he had not been created liable to death or corruption, and the soul was separated from the flesh, that sin might perish by death, not being able to live longer in one dead." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (250-311 AD), Banquet of the Ten Virgins, Discourse 9, Chapter 2
reference: Banquet of the Ten Virgins, Discourse 9, Chapter 2

quote: "But when it came to pass that, by transgressing the commandment (of God), he suffered a terrible and destructive fall, being thus reduced to a state of death, for this reason the Lord says that He came from heaven into (a human) life, leaving the ranks and the armies of angels. For the mountains are to be explained by the heavens, and the ninety and nine sheep by the principalities and powers which the Captain and Shepherd left when He went down to seek the lost one." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (250-311 AD), Banquet of the Ten Virgins, Discourse 3, Chapter 6, Parable of the Lost Sheep Explained
reference: Banquet of the Ten Virgins, Discourse 3, Chapter 6, Parable of the Lost Sheep Explained

quote: "But He set a bound to his [i.e., Adam's] [state of] sin, by interposing death, and thus, causing sin to cease, putting an end to it by the dissolution of the flesh, which should take place in the earth, so that man, ceasing at length to live to sin, and dying to it, might begin to live to God." -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Against Heresies, Book 3, Chapter 23, Paragraph 6
reference: Against Heresies, Book 3, Chapter 23, Paragraph 6

quote: "With Christ, death becomes the bridge which we will cross in an instant in order to continue to live in the unsetting light." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 90
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 90

quote: "God doesn't kill evil. Evil kills itself. God doesn't kill an evil person, but his evil acts lead him to death." -- Saint Paisios (1924-1994 AD), On Spiritual Life, Section 36
reference: On Spiritual Life, Section 36

quote: "By the particular use of our free choice, such impulses of the soul become instruments of virtue or wickedness, just as steel, forged according to the intention of the craftsman, is shaped towards whatever the smith desires, becoming either a sword or some agricultural implement. Therefore if reason, which is the distinctive property of our nature, should gain dominion over those traits which are added to us from outside...none of these impulses would work in us for servitude to evil, but fear would produce obedience in us, anger courage, cowardice caution, and the desiring impulse would mediate to us the divine and immortal pleasure." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 57
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 57

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "These are the traits which, when they occur in us, are called 'passions,' which were not bequeathed to human life solely for evil (for the Creator would bear the blame for evil, if because of them the necessity of transgression had been built into our nature)." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 56
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 56
tags: God is not the author of evil

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "All of these conditions [i.e., the passions] are around the soul and are not the soul itself. They are like warts growing on the mental part of the soul which seem to be parts of it because they grow on it, but they are not what the soul is in its essence." -- Saint Gregory of Nyssa (335-395 AD), On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 54
reference: On the Soul and the Resurrection, Chapter 3, Page 54

quote: "The love of God created us in His image and likeness. He embraced us within the Church in spite of the fact that He knew of our apostasy. He gave us everything to make us gods too through the free gift of grace." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 87
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 87

quote: "In the Church which possesses the saving sacraments there is no despair. We may be deeply sinful. But we make confession, the priest reads the prayer, we are forgiven and we progress towards immortality, without any anxiety and without any fear." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 90
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 90

quote: "Christ united the body of the Church with heaven and with earth: with angels, men and all created things, with all of God's creation - with the animals and birds, with each tiny wild flower and each microscopic insect. The Church thus became 'the fullness of Him who fills all in all [Ephesians 1:23],' that is, of Christ. Everything is in Christ and with Christ. This is the mystery of the Church." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 88
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 88

quote: "No one should wish to be saved alone without all others being saved. It is a mistake for someone to pray for himself, that he himself may be saved. We must love others and pray that no soul be lost, that all may enter into the Church. That is what counts." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 89
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 89

quote: "Devote yourselves to the Scriptures. Love reading and studying them. The more I hear the Psalter and the poetic canons, the more I want to hear them. They are so close-to-life and engaging that I cannot have enough of them. Read clearly and distinctly, word by word." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Monastic Life, Page 163
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Monastic Life, Page 163

quote: "When God bestows on us the gift of humility, then we see all things, we sense all things and we experience God very manifestly. When we do not have humility, we see nothing. On the contrary, when we are made worthy of holy humility, we see all things and rejoice in all things. We experience God and we experience Paradise within ourselves for Paradise is Christ himself." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Divine Providence, Page 193
reference: Wounded By Love, On Divine Providence, Page 193

quote: "That is why we must die to our ancestral humanity and enrobe ourselves in the new humanity. This is what we confess in the sacrament of baptism. With baptism we enter into the joy of Christ. 'As many as are baptized in Christ, have put on Christ [Galatians 2:27].' Confession is a second baptism in which we are purified of our passions, in which our passions are benumbed. Thus divine grace comes through the sacraments." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 134
reference: Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 134

quote: "Pray for others more than for yourself. Say, ‘Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me,’ and you will always have others in your mind. We are all children of the same Father; we are all one. And so, when we pray for others, we say, 'Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me,’ and not, 'have mercy on them'. In this way we make them one with ourselves." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Prayer, Page 132
reference: Wounded By Love, On Prayer, Page 132

quote: "The head of the Church is Christ and we humans, we Christians, are the body. The Apostle Paul says: 'He is the head of the body, of the Church [Colossians 1:18].' The Church and Christ are one. The body cannot exist without its head. The body of the Church is nourished, sanctified and lives with Christ. He is the Lord, omnipotent, omniscient, everywhere present and filling all things, our staff, our friend, our brother: the pillar and sure foundation of the Church. He is the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the basis - everything. Without Christ the Church does not exist. Christ is the Bridegroom; each individual soul is the Bride." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 88
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 88

quote: "Outside the Church, far from the Holy Trinity, we lost Paradise, everything. But outside the Church there is no salvation, there is no life." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 87
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 87

quote: "The Church remains unshaken because she is rooted in the love and wise providence of God." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 87
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Church, Page 87

quote: "Let us stretch out to Him and approach Him as a friend. Do we fall? Do we sin? With familiarity, love, and trust let us run to Him -- not with fear that He will punish us, but with the confidence which we derive from the sense of being with a friend. We can say to Him, 'I have fallen, forgive me.' At the same time, however, let us have the sense that He loves us and that He receives us with tenderness and love and forgives us. Don't let sin separate us from Christ. When we believe that He loves us and we love Him, we don't feel strangers and distanced from Him, even when we sin. We have secured His love, and however we behave, we know that He loves us." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Divine Eros, Page 104
reference: Wounded By Love, On Divine Eros, Page 104

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "'Faith without works is dead [James 2:26],' and the works of faith are: love, peace, long-suffering, mercy, humility, rest from all works (as God Himself rested from His works), bearing of the Cross, and the life in the Spirit. Only such faith can be considered true." -- Saint Seraphim of Sarov (1754-1833 AD), Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 4 - Faith, Paragraph 3
reference: Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 4 - Faith, Paragraph 3

quote: "In times of despondency never fail to bear in mind the Lord's commandment to Peter to forgive a person who sins seventy times seven [Matthew 18:22]. For He who gave this command to another will Himself do far more." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 147
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 147
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "It is one thing to pray for deliverance. From bad thoughts, another to contradict them, another to despise and disregard them...He who stands on the middle step will often make use of the first of these means through being taken unawares. But he who stands on the first step is not in a position to ward off his enemies by the second means. But he who has reached the third step spurns the demons altogether." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 79
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 79
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "When we stand in prayer, those unclean and unspeakable thoughts assail us; but if we continue praying to the end they retire at once, for they do not fight those who stand up to them." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 43
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 43
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "No one in the face of blasphemous thoughts need think that the guilt lies within him, for the Lord is the Knower of hearts and He is aware that such words and thoughts do not come from us but from our foes." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 41
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 41
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "For nothing gives the demons and bad thoughts such power over us as nourishing and hiding them in our heart unconfessed." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 40
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 40
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Unclean and shameful thoughts in the heart are generally produced by the deceiver of the heart, the demon of fornication. But temperance and disregard of them is the cure." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 15, Section 86
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 15, Section 86
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Some have extolled those who are eunuchs by nature because they are delivered from the martyrdom of the body; but I daily extol those who make themselves eunuchs by castrating their bad thoughts as with a knife." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 15, Section 21
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 15, Section 21
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Observe how the thought engendered the feeling, and the thought with the feeling engendered the desire. The mind is filled with passion. All this, however, is still mental impurity and sinfulness. It is still a long way to the act. Between the desire and the act there is always the resolution to act, and premeditation as to how to carry it out...When everything has been premeditated, the resolution is complete. Then the act has already been accomplished within. The sin has already been committed in front of God and the conscience; the commandments have been disregarded, the conscience violated." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 57, Page 239
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 57, Page 239

quote: "Where assent begins [i.e., with passionate thoughts], there also begins guilt, which increases by measure of its involvement in the passionate." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 57, Page 237
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 57, Page 237

quote: "That the passionate [i.e., thoughts] shows itself within us is not an inescapable misfortune. It signifies that we are impure, but it does not make us guilty. Our guilt begins from the point when we favorably incline ourselves toward a passion that has been observed; that is, we do not rush to acknowledge the enemy and do not arm ourselves against it with anger. On the contrary, we accept it and begin liking it, delighting in the impulse in which it appeared." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 57, Page 237
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 57, Page 237

quote: "Do not struggle with passionate thoughts through your own spiritual altercations with them, but turn immediately to the Lord with prayer against them." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 58, Pages 246-247
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 58, Pages 246-247

quote: "It is the property of men to fall, and to rise again as often as this may happen." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 4, Section 31
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 4, Section 31
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Evil thoughts have been engendered from some evil stimulus [i.e., outward influence such as things, people, and events that excite ideas within us]. It is necessary to rush immediately to blout out the stimulus and suppress the thoughts using the method shown earlier [i.e., not giving free reign to our senses: especially the eyes and ears, having prudence, and maintaining inner peace], after the flow of stimuli has been stopped, of course." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 61, Page 258
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 61, Page 258

quote: "Reverent carefulness is necessary here because this sea – that is, the heart, with its thoughts and desires, which one must cleanse by means of mindfulness – is great and vast, and there are numberless reptiles there [Psalm 103:27], that is, numerous vain, unjust, and impure thoughts generated by evil spirits." -- Saint Seraphim of Sarov (1754-1833 AD), Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 7 - The Fear of God
reference: Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 7 - The Fear of God

quote: "They [i.e., those suffering from bad thoughts] think that the corrupt thoughts are their own and therefore they suffer for something which is not their fault but the enemy's." -- Saint Paisios (1924-1994 AD), On Spiritual Life, Section 13
reference: On Spiritual Life, Section 13

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "Please examine yourself thoroughly to see if you have any bad inclinations and passions. Everyone possesses each one of them [i.e., pride, vanity, selfishness, intemperateness, anger, hatred, envy, idleness, desire for sensual pleasures, gloom, and despair] to a small degree, but they are not deeply rooted or permanent. And everyone has one main passion around which all the others entwine themselves. You must take care to seek this one out above all."-- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 35, Pages 161-162
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 35, Pages 161-162

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "In contrast to these dispositions [i.e., humility, contrition, meekness, love of righteousness and truth, mercifulness, pure-heartedness, love of peace, and patience] are the vices or passions, the sources of all the evil deeds that ruin us. The main ones are pride, vanity, selfishness, intemperateness, anger, hatred, envy, idleness, desire for sensual pleasures, gloom, despair. Concerning these, the Apostle decreed that not only should Christians not possess them, but also that they should not mention them among themselves [Ephesians 5:3]." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 35, Page 161
reference: The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned to It, Chapter 35, Page 161

quote: "An evil thought approaches the soul only to tempt and to try a man." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 48, Page 229
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 48, Page 229

quote: "If the enemy decides to attack you with lustful thoughts (according to his usual malice and envy) – don't be put off by it, but use the demon for your own benefit, saying: 'It is good that you have brought me these thoughts – now I am encouraged to pray, otherwise I keep forgetting to pray unceasingly.' Right away the enemy will retreat for he is used to doing only evil." -- Saint Paisios (1924-1994 AD), On Spiritual Life, Section 13
reference: On Spiritual Life, Section 13

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "The failure of hope is the disappearance of love. Toils are bound by it. Labors depend on it. Mercy encircles it." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 30, Section 31
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 30, Section 31
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "He who says that he loves the Lord but is angry with his brother is like a man who dreams that he is running." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 30, Section 27
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 30, Section 27
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "One who loves his neighbor can never tolerate slanderers, but rather runs from them as from fire." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 30, Section 26
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 30, Section 26
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "As love wanes, fear appears; because he who has no fear is either filled with love or dead in soul." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 30, Section 10
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 30, Section 10
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Friends, let us break through this wall of separation [i.e., our sins] which we have erected to our own harm by disobedience; and let us receive the forgiveness of our sins, because in hell there is no one to pardon our debt." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 29, Section 14
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 29, Section 14
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "A king's diadem is not composed of one stone, and dispassion does not reach perfection if we neglect even one virtue, however ordinary." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 29, Section 13
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 29, Section 13
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Some say, moreover, that dispassion is the resurrection of the soul before the body; but others, that it is the perfect knowledge of God, second only to that of the angels." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 29, Section 4
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 29, Section 4
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Ask with tears, seek with obedience, knock with patience. For thus he who asks receives, he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened [Matthew 7:8]." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 56
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 56
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Some say that prayer is better than the remembrance of death, but I praise two natures in one person [i.e., a loving nature (prayer) and a fearful nature (remembrance of death)]." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 46
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 46
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "During prayer do not admit any sensory imagination, so as not to be subject to distraction." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 42
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 42
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "He who is busy with something and continues it when the hour of prayer comes, is deceived by the demons. Those thieves aim at stealing from us one hour after another." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 35
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 35
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Your prayer will show you what condition you are in. Theologians say that prayer is the monk's mirror." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 34
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 34
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Do not say, after spending a long time at prayer, that nothing has been gained; for you have already gained something. And what higher good is there than to cling to the Lord and persevere in unceasing union with Him?" -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 29
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 29
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Faith gives wings to prayer, and without it we cannot fly up to heaven." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 26
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 26
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Prayer is soiled when we stand before God and picture to ourselves irrelevant and inopportune thoughts. Prayer is lost when we are captured by useless cares. Prayer is stolen from us when our thoughts wander before we realize it. Prayer is spoilt by any kind of attack or interruption that comes to us at the time of prayer." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 22
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 22
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Try to lift up, or rather, to shut off your thought within the words of your prayer, and if in its infant state it wearies and falls, lift it up again. Instability is natural to the mind, but God is powerful to establish everything. If you persevere indefatigably in this labor, He who sets the bounds to the sea of the mind will visit you too, and during your prayer will say to the waves: Thus far shalt thou come and no further. Spirit cannot be bound, but where the Creator of the spirit is, everything obeys." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 17
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 17
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)
