quote: "Prayer by reason of its nature is the converse and union of man with God, and by reason of its action upholds the world and brings about reconciliation with God; it is the mother and also the daughter of tears, the propitiation for sins, a bridge over temptations, a wall against afflictions, a crushing of conflicts, work of angels, food of all the spiritual beings, future gladness, boundless activity, the spring of virtues, the source of graces, invisible progress, food of the soul, the enlightening of the mind, an axe for despair, a demonstration of hope, the annulling of sorrow, the wealth of monks, the treasure of solitaries, the reduction of anger, the mirror of progress, the realization of success, a proof of one's condition, a revelation of the future, a sign of glory." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 1
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 1
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "If you feel sweetness or compunction at some word of your prayer, dwell on it; for then our guardian angel is praying with us." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 11
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 11
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Do not attempt to talk much when you pray lest your mind be distracted in searching for words. One word of the publican propitiated God, and one cry of faith saved the thief." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 10
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 10
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Do not be over-sophisticated in the words you use when praying, because the simple and unadorned lisping of children has often won the heart of their heavenly Father." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 9
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 28, Section 9
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "Faith is the wing of prayer; without it, my prayer will return again to my bosom. Faith is the unshaken firmness of the soul, unmoved by any adversity...The mother of faith is hardship and an honest heart; the latter makes faith constant, and the former builds it up." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 27, Section 68
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 27, Section 68
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "What then, does the serpent cast its slough, and shall not we cast off our sin? Thorny ground also, if cultivated well, is turned into fruitful; and is salvation to us irrecoverable? Nay rather, our nature admits of salvation, but the will also is required." -- Saint Cyril of Jerusalem (313-386 AD), Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 2, Section 5
reference: Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 2, Section 5

quote: "Greater than baptism itself is the fountain of tears after baptism, even though it is somewhat audacious to say so. For baptism is the washing away of evils that were in us before, but sins committed after baptism are washed away by tears. As baptism is received in infancy, we have all defiled it, but we cleanse it anew with tears. And if God and His love for mankind had not given us tears, few indeed and hard to find would be those in a state of grace." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 7, Section 6
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 7, Section 6
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "A characteristic of those who are still progressing in blessed mourning is temperance and silence of the lips, and those who have made progress--freedom from anger and patient endurance of injuries; and of the perfect--humility, thirst for dishonours, voluntary craving for involuntary afflictions, noncondemnation of sinners, compassion even beyond one's strength. The first are acceptable, the second laudable; but blessed are those who hunger for hardship and thirst for dishonor, for they shall have their fill of the food that does not cloy." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 7, Section 4
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 7, Section 4
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "God judges our repentance not by our labors but by our humility." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 123
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 123
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Repentance is the renewal of baptism. Repentance is a contract with God for a second life...Repentance is reconciliation with the Lord by the practice of good deeds contrary to the sins." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 5, Section 1
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 5, Section 1
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "What then? Some one will say. We have been beguiled and are lost. Is there then no salvation left? We have fallen: Is it not possible to rise again? We have been blinded: May we not recover our sight? We have become crippled: Can we never walk upright? In a word, we are dead: May we not rise again? He that woke Lazarus who was four days dead and already stank, shall He not, O man, much more easily raise you who art alive? He who shed His precious blood for us, shall Himself deliver us from sin. Let us not despair of ourselves, brethren; let us not abandon ourselves to a hopeless condition. For it is a fearful thing not to believe in a hope of repentance." -- Saint Cyril of Jerusalem (313-386 AD), Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 2, Section 5
reference: Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 2, Section 5

quote: "The testimony of the apostles, who being sent forth by the Lord preached in all the world the Son of God, who came to suffer, and endured to the destruction of death and the quickening of the flesh: that by the putting away of the enmity towards God, which is unrighteousness, we should obtain peace with Him, doing that which is pleasing to Him." -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching, Section 86
reference: Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching, Section 86

quote: "Now, 'the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom [Proverbs 1:7 and Proverbs 9:10];' the sense of sin leads to repentance, and God bestows His compassion upon those who are penitent." -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Against Heresies, Book 3, Chapter 23, Paragraph 5
reference: Against Heresies, Book 3, Chapter 23, Paragraph 5

quote: "Then repentance effaces every sin, when there is no delay after the fall of the soul, and the disease is not suffered to go on through a long interval. For then evil will not have power to leave its mark in us, when it is drawn up at the moment of its being set down like a plant newly planted." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, From the Works of Methodius Against Porphyry, Fragment 2
reference: Fragments, From the Works of Methodius Against Porphyry, Fragment 2

quote: "The approach to God's mercy is open, and the access is easy to those who seek and apprehend the truth. Do you entreat for your sins, although it be in the very end of life, and at the setting of the sun of time; and implore God, who is the one and true God, in confession and faith of acknowledgment of Him, and pardon is granted to the man who confesses, and saving mercy is given from the divine goodness to the believer, and a passage is opened to immortality even in death itself." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 5, Section 25
reference: Treatises, Treatise 5, Section 25

quote: "Nor let any one be restrained either by his sins or by his years from coming to obtain salvation. To him who still remains in this world no repentance is too late." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 5, Section 25
reference: Treatises, Treatise 5, Section 25

quote: "When you have once departed there [i.e., left this earth in death], there is no longer any place for repentance, and no possibility of making satisfaction. Here life is either lost or saved; here eternal safety is provided for by the worship of God and the fruits of faith." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 5, Section 25
reference: Treatises, Treatise 5, Section 25

quote: "But if we also, beloved brethren, are in Christ; if we put Him on, if He is the way of our salvation, who follow Christ in the footsteps of salvation, let us walk by the example of Christ." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 9, Section 9
reference: Treatises, Treatise 9, Section 9

quote: "He still receives His murderers, if they will be converted and come to Him; and with a saving patience, He who is benignant to preserve, closes His Church to none. Those adversaries, those blasphemers, those who were always enemies to His name, if they repent of their sin, if they acknowledge the crime committed, He receives, not only to the pardon of their sin, but to the reward of the heavenly kingdom. What can be said more patient, what more merciful? Even he is made alive by Christ's blood who has shed Christ's blood. Such and so great is the patience of Christ; and had it not been such and so great, the Church would never have possessed Paul as an apostle." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 9, Section 8
reference: Treatises, Treatise 9, Section 8

quote: "But if it is evident that subsequently heresies became more numerous and worse; and if, in time past, it was never at all prescribed nor written that only hands should be laid upon a heretic for repentance, and that so he might be communicated with; and if there is only one baptism, which is with us, and is within, and is granted of the divine condescension to the Church alone, what obstinacy is that, or what presumption, to prefer human tradition [i.e., unwritten traditions for receiving heretics without baptism] to divine ordinance, and not to observe that God is indignant and angry as often as human tradition relaxes and passes by the divine precepts." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 73, Section 3
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 73, Section 3

quote: "For I know not by what presumption some of our colleagues are led to think that they who have been dipped by heretics ought not to be baptized when they come to us, for the reason that they say that there is one baptism which indeed is therefore one, because the Church is one, and there cannot be any baptism out of the Church. For since there cannot be two baptisms, if heretics truly baptize, they themselves have this baptism...But we say that those who come thence are not re-baptized among us, but are baptized. For indeed they do not receive anything there [i.e., from being baptized by a heretic], where there is nothing; but they come to us, that here they may receive where there is both grace and all truth, because both grace and truth are one. But again some of our colleagues would rather give honour to heretics than agree with us; and while by the assertion of one baptism they are unwilling to baptize those that come, they thus either themselves make two baptisms in saying that there is a baptism among heretics; or certainly, which is a matter of more importance, they strive to set before and prefer the sordid and profane washing of heretics to the true and only and legitimate baptism of the Catholic Church, not considering that it is written, 'He who is baptized by one dead, what avails his washing [Sirach 34:25]?' Now it is manifest that they who are not in the Church of Christ are reckoned among the dead; and another cannot be made alive by him who himself is not alive, since there is one Church which, having attained the grace of eternal life, both lives for ever and quickens the people of God." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 70, Section 1
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 70, Section 1

quote: "But if he who comes from the heretics has not previously been baptized in the Church, but comes as a stranger and entirely profane, he must be baptized, that he may become a sheep, because in the holy Church is the one water which makes sheep. And therefore, because there can be nothing common to falsehood and truth, to darkness and light, to death and immortality, to Antichrist and Christ, we ought by all means to maintain the unity of the Catholic Church, and not to give way to the enemies of faith and truth in any respect." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 70, Section 2
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 70, Section 2

quote: "Although Novatian himself, whom he [i.e., Marcianus of Arles] follows, has formerly been excommunicated, and judged an enemy to the Church; and when he sent ambassadors to us into Africa, asking to be received into our communion, he received back word from a council of several priests who were here present, that he himself had excluded himself, and could not by any of us be received into communion, as he had attempted to erect a profane altar, and to set up an adulterous throne, and to offer sacrilegious sacrifices opposed to the true priest." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 66, Section 2
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 66, Section 2

quote: "For these things [i.e., deacons disobeying and contending with their priests and bishops] are the beginnings of heretics, and the origins and endeavors of evil-minded schismatics;—to please themselves, and with swelling haughtiness to despise him who is set over them. Thus they depart from the Church—thus a profane altar is set up outside—thus they rebel against the peace of Christ, and the appointment and the unity of God." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 64, Section 3
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 64, Section 3

quote: "But deacons ought to remember that the Lord chose apostles, that is, bishops and overseers; while apostles appointed for themselves deacons after the ascent of the Lord into heaven, as ministers of their episcopacy and of the Church." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 64, Section 3
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 64, Section 3

quote: "The highest degree of happiness is, not to sin; the second, to acknowledge our sins. In the former, innocence flows pure and unstained to preserve us; in the latter, there comes a medicine to heal us." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 54, Section 13
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 54, Section 13

quote: "For our own part, it befits our conscience, dearest brother, to strive that none should perish going out of the Church by our fault; but if any one, of his own accord and by his own sin, should perish, and should be unwilling to repent and to return to the Church, that we who are anxious for their well-being should be blameless in the day of judgment, and that they alone should remain in punishment who refused to be healed by the wholesomeness of our advice." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 54, Section 8
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 54, Section 8

quote: "But apostates and deserters, or adversaries and enemies, and those who lay waste the Church of Christ, cannot, even if outside the Church they have been slain for His name, according to the apostle, be admitted to the peace of the Church, since they have neither kept the unity of the spirit nor of the Church." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 51, Section 29
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 51, Section 29

quote: "Certainly the Lord would not exhort to repentance, if it were not that He promises mercy to them that repent." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 51, Section 22
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 51, Section 22

quote: "For since it is written, 'God did not make death, neither has He pleasure in the destruction of the living [Wisdom 1:13],' assuredly He who wills that none should perish, desires that sinners should repent, and by repentance should return again to life." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 51, Section 22
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 51, Section 22

quote: "But I wonder that some are so obstinate as to think that repentance is not to be granted to the lapsed, or to suppose that pardon is to be denied to the penitent, when it is written, 'Remember whence you are fallen, and repent, and do the first works [Revelation 2:5],' which certainly is said to him who evidently has fallen, and whom the Lord exhorts to rise up again by his works, because it is written, 'Alms do deliver from death [Tobit 4:10]'." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 51, Section 22
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 51, Section 22

quote: "We have an advocate and an intercessor for our sins, Jesus Christ the Lord and our God, if only we repent of our sins past, and confess and acknowledge our sins, whereby we now offend the Lord, and for the time to come engage to walk in His ways, and to fear His commandments." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 7, Section 5
reference: Epistles of Cyprian of Carthage, Epistle 7, Section 5

quote: "Standing fast in non-scriptural tradition is, I think, apostolic. For it is written, 'I praise you that you remember me in all things, and hold fast to the traditions just as I have handed on to you [1 Corinthians 11:2].' And, 'Keep the traditions that you have received, either by word or by letter [2 Thessalonians 2:15].' One of these traditions is the one now under discussion [i.e., giving glory with the Spirit], which those, who arranged it from the beginning and handed it over to their successors (its use ever advancing in time), implanted in the churches by long custom." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 29, Section 71, Paragraph 1
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 29, Section 71, Paragraph 1

quote: "In the same way, the apostles and fathers ordained from the first the matters of the Church and guarded the solemnity of the mysteries in secrecy and silence, for what is made known for a public and casual hearing is no mystery at all. This is the reason for non-scriptural traditions, that knowledge of dogmas not be neglected or despised by the many because of familiarity." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 27, Section 66, Paragraph 3
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 27, Section 66, Paragraph 3

quote: "For if we attempt to reject non-scriptural customs as insignificant, we would, unaware, lose the very vital parts of the Gospel, and even more, we would establish the proclamation merely in name. For instance--I will mention the first and most common--who has learned through the Scriptures that those who hope in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ are marked with the sign of the cross? What sort of scriptural text teaches us to turn to the East for prayer? Which saint has left us a scriptural account of the words of the epiclesis at the manifestation of the bread of the Eucharist and the cup of blessing?...We bless the water of Baptism and the oil of chrism in addition to the very one who is to be baptized. By what scriptures? Is it not by the secret and mystical tradition? But why? What scriptural authority teaches the anointing itself of oil? Where does a man being immersed three times come from? How much of the baptismal ritual is for the renunciation of Satan and his angels, and what scriptual text does it come from?Does it not come from this secret and unspoken teaching, which our fathers guarded with a simple and unprying silence, since they were all taught the solemnity of the mysteries is preserved by silence." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 27, Section 66, Paragraph 1
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 27, Section 66, Paragraph 1

quote: "Of the dogmas and proclamations that are guarded in the Church, we hold some from the teaching of the Scriptures, and others we have received in mystery as the teachings of the tradition of the apostles. Both hold the same power with respect to true religion. No one would deny these points, at least no one who has even a little experience of ecclesiastical institutions." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 27, Section 66, Paragraph 1
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 27, Section 66, Paragraph 1

quote: "Our God and Savior's plan for man is his restoration from the fall and his return from the alienation of disobedience to kinship with God. For the sake of this are Christ's sojourn in the flesh, His example of an evangelical way of life, His sufferings, His cross, His burial, His Resurrection. And so the man who is saved receives back that original adopted sonship by imitating Christ. The imitation of Christ, accordingly, is necessary for the perfection of life, not only in His living example of humility, patience, and freedom from anger, but also in that of His very death...How, then, are we made in the likeness of His death? We were buried with Him through Baptism." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 15, Section 35, Paragraphs 1-2
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 15, Section 35, Paragraphs 1-2

quote: "For the invocation of Christ [i.e., in Baptism] is the confession of the whole [i.e., the Trinity], since it is clear that God is the One anointing, the Son is the One anointed, and the Spirit is the anointing, as we have learned from Peter in Acts. 'Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit [Acts 10:38].' And in Isaiah, 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He anointed me [Isaiah 61:1].' And the psalmist says, 'On account of this, God, Your God, anointed You with the oil of gladness [Psalm 44:8].' In fact, sometimes he appears to make mention only of the Holy Spirit at Baptism. 'For we all,' he says, 'were baptized in one body into one Spirit [1 Corinthians 12:13].' The following text agrees with this one: 'Now you were baptized in the Holy Spirit [Acts 1:5],' and, 'He Himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit [Luke 3:16].' But no one would say, according to this, that Baptism is complete in which only the name of the Spirit was invoked. For the tradition that has been given in life-giving grace must always remain unchanged...So to add or subtract anything is plainly the loss of eternal life." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 12, Section 28, Paragraphs 1-2
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 12, Section 28, Paragraphs 1-2

quote: "Well, then, if the separation of the Spirit from the Father and the Son in Baptism is dangerous for the baptizer and useless for the baptized, how is it safe for us to separate the Spirit from the Father and the Son? Now faith and Baptism are two ways of salvation that are naturally united with each other and indivisible. While faith is perfected by Baptism, Baptism is established by faith, and each is carried out by the same names. For as we believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so also we are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The confession that brings salvation comes first and there follows Baptism which seals our assent." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 12, Section 28, Paragraph 3
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 12, Section 28, Paragraph 3

quote: "Who is so contentious, who is so devoid of the heavenly gift, who has had so little a taste of the beautiful words of God, who is so bereft of everlasting hope, that he removes the Spirit from the Godhead and ranks Him with creation?" -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 24, Section 56, Paragraph 1
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 24, Section 56, Paragraph 1

quote: "To what kind of Lord does he pray will fix the hearts of the faithful in Thessalonica blamelessly steadfast in holiness before our God and Father, in the presence of our Lord [1 Thessalonians 3:12-13]? Let those who place the Holy Spirit among the ministering spirits sent for service answer us. They have no answer." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 21, Section 52, Paragraph 2
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 21, Section 52, Paragraph 2

quote: "We find, accordingly, the following texts with the Apostle: 'may the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and into Christ's endurance' of afflictions [2 Thessalonians 3:5]. Who is the Lord directing into the love of God and into Christ's endurance of afflictions? Let those who reduce the Spirit to slavery answer us. For if the verse had been about God the Father, it would no doubt have said, 'may the Lord direct you into the love of Himself.' And if it had been about the Son, there would have followed, 'into His Own endurance.' Let them, then, find out what other person is worthy to be honoured with the title Lord." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 21, Section 52, Paragraph 2
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 21, Section 52, Paragraph 2

quote: "We do not count them as a group, making for ourselves an increase from one to many and saying 'one, two, three.' Neither do we say 'first, second, third.'...By worshipping God from God, we confess the particularizing property of the persons and we stay within the monarchy...And so, with regard to the particularity of the persons, they are one and one, but with regard to the common nature, both are one thing. How, then, if they are one in one are there not two gods? Because it is said that there is a king and the image of the king, but not two kings, for the power is not divided, and the glory is not portioned out. As the power that rules over us and the authority is one, so also one, not many, is the doxology from us. On account of this, the honor of the image passes over to the archetype. Therefore, the image is the prototype by way of imitation [in the case of the king and his image]; the Son is this by nature. And just as in the arts there is a likeness according to form, so with a divine and incomposite nature, the unity is in the communion of the Godhead." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 18, Section 45, Paragraph 1
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 18, Section 45, Paragraph 1

quote: "Do you say that the Son also is numbered under the Father, and the Spirit, under the Son, or do you limit sub-numeration to the Spirit alone? For if you sub-numerate the Son too, you renew again the same impious position--namely, the unlikeness of His substance, the lowering of His dignity, His generation at a later time--and generally you admit at once all the blasphemies against the Son by turning back through this one word...Generally speaking, what thing ever loses its own nature when it is counted? Rather, is it not the case that things counted remain in the sort of things that they have been by nature from the beginning, while we use number as a knowable sign of a plurality of substances?" -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 17, Section 43, Paragraphs 1-2
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 17, Section 43, Paragraphs 1-2

quote: "For if He [i.e., Christ] is without difference in substance [i.e., with the Father], He will also be without difference in power, and for those whose power is identical, the energy also is wholly identical. For 'Christ is the power of God and wisdom of God [1 Corinthians 1:24]'. And 'all things were made through Him [John 1:3],' and 'all things were created through Him and for Him [Colossians 1:16].' He does not perform the instrumental service of some slave, but perfectly fulfils the creative will of the Father." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 8, Section 19, Paragraph 3
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 8, Section 19, Paragraph 3

quote: "What just defense will we have at the fearful last judgment of all creation, if we force Him Who has been enthroned and given equal honor to come down from His position of equality, when the Lord has plainly proclaimed that He has come, 'in the glory of the Father [Matthew 16:23],' when Stephen saw 'Jesus standing at the right hand of God [Acts 7:55],' when Paul, called to witness to Christ in the Spirit, says that He 'is at the right hand of God [Romans 8:34],' when the Father says, 'Sit at My right hand [Psalm 109:1],' and when the Holy Spirit testifies that 'He sits at the right hand...of the majesty' of God [Hebrews 8:1]? The 'standing' and the 'sitting' in these texts shows, I think, solidity and absolute stability of His nature, just as Baruch illustrated the unmoving and immutable character of God's mode of existence when he said, 'You sit forever, and we perish forever [Baruch 3:3].' 'At the right hand,' I think, indicates an equality of honor and dignity. How, then, is it not audacious to rob the Son of His communion [with the Father] in the doxology, as if He deserved to be ranked in a lower place of honor?" -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 6, Section 15, Paragraph 3
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 6, Section 15, Paragraph 3

quote: "'He who does not honor the Son, does not honor the Father [John 5:23]'--how is it pious for these men [i.e., heretics] not to worship and glorify with the Father Him Who has been united to the Father in nature, in glory, and in dignity?" -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 6, Section 15, Paragraph 3
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 6, Section 15, Paragraph 3

quote: "The hair-splitting reasoning of these men [i.e., heretics] concerning syllables and words is not a simple matter, as it might seem, and it results in no small evil. Rather, this reasoning is profoundly and malevolently opposed to true religion. For they love to win an argument and to point out the different expressions of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit." -- Saint Basil the Great (330-379 AD), On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 2, Section 4, Paragraph 1
reference: On the Holy Spirit, Chapter 2, Section 4, Paragraph 1

quote: "Fellowship with despondency would seem like adultery to anyone who is united to God." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 27, Section 29
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 27, Section 29
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Lack of obedience is due to egotism and self-love. Egotism and pride engendered the disobedience which ejected us from Paradise." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On The Monastic Life, Page 163
reference: Wounded By Love, On The Monastic Life, Page 163

quote: "You must pass through obedience to be a complete person, in order to face the difficulties of human life. Without humility and without obedience, you do not have the grace of God." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On The Monastic Life, Page 163
reference: Wounded By Love, On The Monastic Life, Page 163

quote: "Obedience is very important. It is a great virtue and is the same as humility. Obedience with joy and willingness - even if what your elder demands is wrong-headed. Obedience as such is of great value. Such obedience is touching to God: 'I love those who love Me, and those who seek Me shall find grace [Proverbs 8:17]'." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On The Monastic Life, Page 161
reference: Wounded By Love, On The Monastic Life, Page 161

quote: "Obedience is a great and wise thing. It is the secret of spiritual life. We are unable to comprehend it." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On The Monastic Life, Page 161
reference: Wounded By Love, On The Monastic Life, Page 161

quote: "Complete trust in God - that's what holy humility is. Complete obedience to God, without protest, without reaction, even when some things seem difficult and unreasonable. Abandonment to the hands of God." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 152
reference: Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 152

quote: "To enter into this 'frame of mind', start with obedience. You must submit first to obedience in order for humility to come. When He sees humility, the Lord sends divine grace and then prayer supervenes on its own, effortlessly. If you don't submit to obedience and don't have humility, the prayer [i.e., the Jesus Prayer] doesn't come and there is a danger of being led into error and delusion. Prepare yourself gradually and gently and repeat the prayer in your mind." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Prayer, Page 119
reference: Wounded By Love, On Prayer, Page 119

quote: "If we wish to follow Him, then this life, too, with Christ, is joy, even amid difficulties. As Saint Paul says, 'I rejoice in my sufferings [Colossians 1:24].' This is our religion, and that's the direction we must move in. It is not the outward formalities that count; it is living with Christ that matters. When you achieve this, what else do you want? You have gained everything. You live in Christ and Christ lives in you. Thereafter everything is easy: obedience, humility and peace." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Divine Eros, Page 105
reference: Wounded By Love, On Divine Eros, Page 105

quote: "Obedience shows love for Christ. And Christ especially loves the obedient. That's why He says, ‘I love those who love Me, and those who seek Me will find grace [Proverbs 8:17]’." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, The Holy Mountain - Kavsokalyvia, Page 24
reference: Wounded By Love, The Holy Mountain - Kavsokalyvia, Page 24

quote: "This blessed obedience benefited me greatly. It changed me. I became sharp-witted, quick and stronger in body and soul. It made me know everything. I must glorify God day and night for granting me the possibility of living in this way in this life." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, The Holy Mountain - Kavsokalyvia, Page 24
reference: Wounded By Love, The Holy Mountain - Kavsokalyvia, Page 24

quote: "Obedience! What can I say? I truly knew the meaning of that word! I abandoned myself to obedience with joy and love. It was this absolute obedience that saved me and it was on account of this that God gave me His charismatic gift." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, The Holy Mountain - Kavsokalyvia, Page 12
reference: Wounded By Love, The Holy Mountain - Kavsokalyvia, Page 12

quote: "'They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick; I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance [Luke 5:31-32].' How then shall the sick be strengthened, or how shall sinners come to repentance? Is it by a persevering in the very same courses? Or, on the contrary, is it by undergoing a great change and reversal of their former mode of living?" -- Saint Irenaeus (120-200 AD), Against Heresies, Book 3, Chapter 5, Paragraph 2
reference: Against Heresies, Book 3, Chapter 5, Paragraph 2

quote: "The true light does not shine in all human hearts in the same way. Natural sunlight shines the same everywhere, but the rays of light do not penetrate far into a house that has dirty windows. The same happens with the uncreated light. If our windows are dirty and our heart is not pure then the blackness does not allow the rays to penetrate." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 140
reference: Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 140

quote: "Those who have been humbled by their passions may take courage. For even if they fall into every pit and are trapped in all the snares and suffer all maladies, yet after their restoration to health they become physicians, beacons, lamps, and pilots for all, teaching us the habits of every disease and from their own personal experience able to prevent their neighbors from falling." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 13
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 13
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "For many sects have had birth, since their time, holding opinions opposed to their [i.e., the Apostles] words; whereof some have received all that they have said while some have cut off from the rest certain portions of their statements, and so retain them for theirselves...And like as if thou shouldest take any part from the side of an animal, even in that part thou wouldest find all the things out of which the whole is composed;--nerves and veins, bones, arteries, and blood, and a sample, as one might say, of the whole lump;--so likewise with regard to the Scriptures; in each portion of what is there stated, one may see the connection with the whole clearly appearing...and the doctrine itself had long since been brought to nought: 'for every kingdom', saith He, 'divided against itself shall not stand [Matthew 12:25]'." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Matthew, Homily 1, Section 8
reference: Homilies on Matthew, Homily 1, Section 8

quote: “Those whose mind has learned true prayer converse with the Lord face to face, as if speaking into the ear of the Emperor. Those who make vocal prayer fall down before Him as if in the presence of the whole senate. But those who live in the world petition the Emperor amidst the clamor of all the crowds.” -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 27, Section 21
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 27, Section 21
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "The first thing to do in making repentance is to go inside yourself. Earthly matters and cares and unrestrained wandering of thoughts all over the place do not allow us to go inside ourselves and to study ourselves." -- Saint Theophan the Recluse (1815-1894 AD), The Spiritual Life and How to Be Attuned To It, 32. Govenie: The Path of a Virtuous Life, Page 150
reference: The Spiritual Life and How To Be Attuned to It, Chapter 32, Page 150

quote: "Let us love God at least as much as we respect our friends. For I have often seen people who had offended God and were not in the least perturbed about it. And I have seen how those same people provoked their friends in some trifling matter and then employed every artifice, every device, every sacrifice, every apology, both personally and through friends and relatives, not sparing gifts, in order to regain their former love." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 1, Section 15
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 1, Section 15
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: “There is no unpardonable sin, save the unrepented one.” -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 2, Page 10
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 2, Page 10

quote: "Talkativeness is the throne of vainglory on which it loves to show itself and make a display. Talkativeness is a sign of ignorance, a door to slander, a guide to jesting, a servant of falsehood, the ruin of compunction, a creator of despondency, a precursor of sleep, the dissipation of recollection, the abolition of watchfulness, the cooling of ardor, the darkening of prayer." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 11, Section 2
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 11, Section 2
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "When you hear that your neighbor or friend has abused you behind your back or even to your face, then show love and praise him." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 22, Section 15
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 22, Section 15
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "He who wants to overcome the spirit of slander should not ascribe the blame to the person who falls, but to the demon who suggests it." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 5
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 5
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "I have heard people slandering others, and I have rebuked them. Then these doers of evil replied in self-defense that they were doing so out of love and care for the person whom they were judging. I said to them: 'Stop that kind of love, otherwise you will be condemning the prophet David as a liar who said: ‘whoever speaks secretly against his neighbor, I have driven away from me [Psalm 100:5]’. If you say you love, then pray secretly, and do not mock the man. For this is the kind of love that is acceptable to the Lord.'" -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 4
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 4
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Slander is an offspring of hatred, a subtle yet coarse disease, a leech lurking unfelt, wasting and draining the blood of charity. It is simulation of love, the patron of a heavy and unclean heart, the ruin of chastity." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 2
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 2
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Do not judge too severely those who are eloquent and preaching but do not support this in practice, for the profit of a word has often compensated for the dearth of deeds. We do not all obtain everything in equal measure. With some speech takes precedence over action, but with others the latter transcends the former." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 155
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 155
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "What is the sign that a man has attained to purity of heart, and when does a man know that his heart has entered into purity? When he sees all men as good and none appears to him to be unclean and defiled. Then in very truth his heart is pure." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 37, Page 177
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 37, Page 177

quote: "He who hates his sins will cease to sin, and he who confesses them will receive forgiveness. It is impossible for a man to forsake the habit of sin if he does not first acquire a hatred of sin; and it is impossible to receive forgiveness before a confession of iniquities. With the latter (i.e. confession) there is real abasement, and with the former (i.e. hatred of sin) there is remorse arising from shame that cleaves to the heart." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 32, Page 152
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 32, Page 152

quote: "Do not regard the feelings of a person who speaks to you about his neighbor disparagingly, but rather say to him: 'Stop, brother! I fall into graver sins every day, so how can I criticize him?'" -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 7
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 7
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "If you see someone falling into sin at the very moment of his death, even then do not judge him, because the Divine judgment is hidden from men. Some have fallen openly into great sins, but they have done greater good deeds in secret; so their critics were tricked." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 8
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 10, Section 8
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "We must not judge anyone, even if with our own eyes we have seen someone sinning, or walking in transgression of God's commandments. For according to the word of God: Judge not, that ye be not judged [Matthew 7:1]." -- Saint Seraphim of Sarov (1754-1833 AD), Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 20 - Do Not Judge Your Neighbor, Paragraph 1
reference: Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 20 - Do Not Judge Your Neighbor, Paragraph 1

quote: "He who busies himself with the sins of others, or judges his brother on suspicion, has not yet even begun to repent or to examine himself so as to discover his own sins." -- Saint Maximus the Confessor (580-662 AD), Philokalia (Vol. I), Four Hundred Texts on Love, Third Century, Section 55
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), Four Hundred Texts on Love, Third Century, Section 55

quote: "If you guard your tongue, my brother, God will give you the gift of compunction of heart so that you may see your soul, and thereby you will enter into spiritual joy. But if your tongue defeats you—believe me in what I say to you—you will never be able to escape from darkness. If you do not have a pure heart, at least have a pure mouth, as the blessed John said" -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 48, Page 236
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 48, Page 236

quote: "If you compel your body when it is weak to labors that exceed its strength, you will instill darkness upon darkness into your soul and bring greater confusion upon her." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 48, Page 235
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 48, Page 235

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "Faith produces fear in us, and fear compels us to repent and to set ourselves to work." -- Saint Issac the Syrian, Ascetical Homilies, Homily 47, Page 227
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 47, Page 227

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "One must not nurse in one's heart malice or hatred towards a neighbor who bears ill-will; but we must strive to love him and, as much as possible, do good, following the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ: Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you [Matthew 5:44]." -- Saint Seraphim of Sarov (1754-1833 AD), Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 21 - Forgiveness of Offenses, Paragraph 2
reference: Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 21 - Forgiveness of Offenses, Paragraph 2

quote: "I can't give you an example of what real obedience is. It's not that we have a discussion about the virtue of obedience and then I say to you, go and do a somersault, and you obey. That's not obedience. You need to be entirely carefree and not thinking at all about the matter of obedience, and then suddenly you are asked to do something and you are ready to do it joyfully." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, The Holy Mountain - Kavsokalyvia, Page 19
reference: Wounded By Love, The Holy Mountain - Kavsokalyvia, Page 19

quote: "When you praise children constantly and indiscriminately, they fall prey to the temptations of the evil one. He sets the mill of egotism in motion, and accustomed as they are to praise from their parents and teachers, they make progress at school perhaps, but what is the gain? In life they will be egotists and not Christians. Egotists can never be Christians. Egotists desire to be praised constantly by everyone, for everyone to love them, and for everyone to speak, well of them and this is something that our God, our Church, and our Christ do not want." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 208
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 208

quote: "Pray and then speak. That's what to do with your children. If you are constantly lecturing them, you'll become tiresome and when they grow up, they'll feel a kind of oppression. Prefer prayer and speak to them through prayer. Speak to God and God will speak to their hearts." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 203
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 203

quote: "Silence saves us from all evils. Restraint of the tongue is a great thing. In a mystical way silence radiates out to our neighbour." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Love for One's Neighbor, Page 184
reference: Wounded By Love, On Love for One's Neighbor, Page 184

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "Love needs to be sincere. And only the love of God is sincere love. To a person whom we find tiresome and troublesome, love needs to be offered in a subtle manner without the person being aware that we are striving to love him. It shouldn't be given much outward expression, because then the person will react." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Love for One's Neighbor, Page 184
reference: Wounded By Love, On Love for One's Neighbor, Page 184

quote: "A [parent] should not be satisfied by giving her child a physical caress, but should also coddle it with a caress of prayer." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Pages 199-200
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Pages 199-200

quote: "[Parents] who are always standing over their children and pressurizing them, that is over-protecting them, have failed in their task. You need to leave the child alone to take an interest in its own progress. Then you will succeed. When you are always standing over them, the children react. They become lethargic and weak-willed and generally are unsuccessful in life. This is a kind of over-protectiveness that leaves the children immature." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 199
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 199

quote: "Parents...often cause hurt to a child for some act of misbehavior by scolding them excessively. The child is then wounded. Even if you don't scold the child outwardly, but bristle with anger inwardly or look fiercely at the child, the child understands." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 198
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 198

quote: "Generally the parents are to blame for the bad behavior of the children. And their behavior is not improved by reprimands, disciplining, or strictness. If the parents do not pursue a life of holiness and if they don't engage in spiritual struggle, they make great mistakes and transmit the faults they have within them. If the parents do not live a holy life and do not display love towards each other, the devil torments the parents with the reactions of the children." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 196
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Upbringing of Children, Page 196

quote: "He who wants to grapple with the demon of blasphemy in any other way is like a man trying to hold lightning in his hands. For how will you catch, or contend and grapple with one who bursts into the heart suddenly like the wind, utters words quicker than a flash, and immediately vanishes? All other enemies stop, wrestle, linger and give time to those who wish to struggle with them. But not this one: he has scarcely appeared, and he is gone; he has hardly said a word, and he is away." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 47
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 47
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "He who is troubled by the spirit of blasphemy and wants to be delivered from it should know for certain that it is not his soul that is the cause of such thoughts but the impure demon who once said to the Lord: 'All these things will I give Thee if Thou wilt fall down and worship me [Matthew 4:9].' And so let us too humiliate him and,  without paying the least regard to his suggestion, say to him: 'Get thee behind me, Satan! I shall worship the Lord my God, and Him only will I serve [Matthew 4:10]. Thy labor and thy word will return upon thy head, and thy blasphemies will come down upon thy crown [Psalm 7:17] in the present and in the future world. Amen'." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 46
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 46
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "A most learned old man spiritually admonished a proud brother, but he in his blindness said: 'Excuse me, Father, I am not proud.' The wise old man said to him: 'What clear proof of this passion could you have given us, son, than to say, "I am not proud"?'" -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 14
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 23, Section 14
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Those who consider it a misfortune to lose children, slaves, money or any other of their belongings, must realize that in the first place they should be satisfied with what is given them by God; and then, when they have to give it back, they should be ready to do so gratefully, without any indignation at being deprived of it, or rather at giving it back - for since they have been enjoying the use of what was not their own, they are now in fact returning it." -- Saint Anthony the Great (251-356 AD), Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life, One Hundred and Seventy Texts, Section 36
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life, One Hundred and Seventy Texts, Section 36

quote: "There is no profit in studying doctrines unless the life of one's soul is acceptable and conforms to God's will. The cause of all evils is delusion, self-deception and ignorance of God." -- Saint Anthony the Great (251-356 AD), Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life, One Hundred and Seventy Texts, Section 26
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life, One Hundred and Seventy Texts, Section 26

quote: "Intelligent men have no need to listen to much talk, but should attend only to that which is profitable and guided by God's will. For in this way men regain life and eternal light." -- Saint Anthony the Great (251-356 AD), Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life, One Hundred and Seventy Texts, Section 24
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life, One Hundred and Seventy Texts, Section 24

quote: "Someone asked one of those who could see: 'Why does God, who foresees their falls, adorn some with gifts and wonder-working powers?' And he replied: 'In order to make other Spiritual men more careful, and to demonstrate the freedom of the human will, and to cause those who fall to be without any excuse at the last judgment.'" -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 131
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 131
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "The lessening of evil breeds abstinence from evil; and abstinence from evil is the beginning of repentance; and the beginning of repentance is the beginning of salvation; and the beginning of salvation is a good intention; and a good intention is the mother of labors. And the beginning of labors is the virtues; the beginning of the virtues is a flowering, and the flowering of virtue is the beginning of activity. And the offspring of virtue is perseverance; and the fruit and offspring of persevering practice is habit, and the child of habit is character. Good character is the mother of fear; and fear gives birth to the keeping of commandments in which I include both heavenly and earthly. The keeping of the commandments is a sign of love; and the beginning of love is an abundance of humility; and an abundance of humility is the daughter of dispassion; and the acquisition of the latter is the fullness of love, that is to say the perfect indwelling of God in those who through dispassion are pure in heart. For they shall see God [Matthew 5:8]. And to Him the glory for all eternity. Amen." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Brief Summary of All the Previous Steps, Section 65
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Brief Summary of All the Previous Steps, Section 65
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Conscious perception produces either the cessation or lessening of evil; and it is the offspring of conscience. And conscience is the word and conviction of our guardian angel given to us from the time of baptism. That is why we find that the unbaptized do not feel such keen pangs of remorse in their soul for their bad deeds." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Brief Summary of All the Previous Steps, Section 64
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Brief Summary of All the Previous Steps, Section 64
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "To yield and give way to our passions is the lowest slavery, even as to rule over them is the only liberty." -- Saint Justin Martyr (100-165 AD), Fragments of St. Justin Martyr, Fragment 18
reference: Fragments of St. Justin Martyr, Fragment 18

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "As one who has suffered a prolonged illness can scarcely obtain health in an instant, so it is impossible suddenly to overcome the passions, or even one passion." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Brief Summary of All the Previous Steps, Section 55
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Brief Summary of All the Previous Steps, Section 55
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "When our praisers, or rather our seducers, begin to praise us, let us briefly call to mind the multitude of our sins, and we shall find ourselves unworthy of what is said or done in our honor." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 22, Section 42
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 22, Section 42
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "He who has piously destroyed within him the three passions [i.e., gluttony, cupidity (extreme greed), and vainglory] has destroyed the five [i.e., lust, anger, despair, despondency, and pride] too; but he who has been negligent about the former will not conquer even one passion." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 2
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 2
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "At the moment of temptation, the easiest thing to do is to turn to your loved one, to God, and to look to Him steadfastly and expectantly and you will be filled with strength at once. As soon as you see evil coming to get you, ignore it and run to God's embrace...And so when you go towards good, you cease to remember evil." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 151
reference: Wounded By Love, On Spiritual Struggle, Page 151

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "Some say that we fall into the same sins because we have been unable to correct our former sins through the inadequacy of our repentance. But it may be asked: Have all those who have not fallen into the same kind of sin really repented as they should? Some fall into the same sins either because they have sunk into a deep forgetfulness of their former sins, or because they imagine in their own pleasure-loving way that God is merciful, or they have lost all hope and their own salvation. I do not know whether anyone will blame me if I say that their trouble arises because they have not been strong enough to bind the foe who is dominating them through the tyranny of habit." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 171
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 171
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "If you wish to be in control of your soul and body, forestall the passions by rooting out their causes." -- Saint Thalassios the Libyan (died 648 AD), Philokalia (Vol. II), On Love, Self-control and Life in Accordance with the Intellect, First Century, Section 64
reference: Philokalia (Vol. II), On Love, Self-control and Life in Accordance with the Intellect, First Century, Section 64

quote: "One should always endure any trial for the sake of God with gratitude. Our life is a single minute in comparison with eternity; and therefore, according to the Apostle, 'the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us [Romans 8:18]'." -- Saint Seraphim of Sarov (1754-1833 AD), Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 16 - Patience and Humility, Paragraph 1
reference: Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 16 - Patience and Humility, Paragraph 1

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "True faith cannot be without works; one who truly believes will unfailingly have works as well." -- Saint Seraphim of Sarov (1754-1833 AD), Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 4 - Faith, Paragraph 3
reference: Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 4 - Faith, Paragraph 3

quote: "He allows the tempter to remain with us and for as long as we must wait to be revived through patience and secure passionlessness!" --  Saint Seraphim of Sarov (1754-1833 AD), Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 14 - Despair, Paragraph 2
reference: Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 14 - Despair, Paragraph 2

quote: "We have received from God self-control, forbearance, restraint, fortitude, patience, and the like, which are great and holy powers, helping us to resist the enemy's attacks. If we cultivate these powers and have them at our disposal, we do not regard anything that befalls us as painful, grievous or unbearable, realizing that it is human and can be overcome by the virtues within us. The unintelligent do not take this into account; they do not understand that all things happen for our benefit, rightly and as they should, so that our virtues may shine and we ourselves be crowned by God" -- Saint Anthony the Great (251-356 AD), Philokalia, On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life, One Hundred and Seventy Texts, Section 3
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Character of Men and on the Virtuous Life, One Hundred and Seventy Texts, Section 3

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "Some of the faithful, and even of the unfaithful, have been deserted by the passions, all except one; and that one has been left as a paramount evil which fully takes the place of all the others, for it is so harmful that it can even cast down from heaven." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 62
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 62
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "The mother of lust is gluttony, and the mother of despondency is vainglory; sorrow and also anger are the offspring of those three (i.e., cupidity, sensuality, ambition); and the mother of pride is vain glory." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 39
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 39
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Do you see what great profit arises to us from the poor? Should you take them away, you would take away the great hope of our salvation." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Matthew, Homily 78, Section 2
reference: Homilies on Matthew, Homily 78, Section 2

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "Love sinners, but hate their works; and do not despise them for their faults, lest you be tempted by the same." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 5, Page 51
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 5, Page 51

quote: "In the case of those who malevolently dispute with us, whether unbelievers or heretics, we should desist after we have twice admonished them [Titus 3:10]. But in the case of those who wish to learn the truth let us never grow weary in well-doing [Galatians 6:9]. However, we should use both opportunities for the establishment of our own heart [Hebrews 13:9]." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 125
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 125
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Be attentive also to your insignificant falls. If from inattentiveness some sin happens with you, do not despair but immediately take yourself in hand and fall down before God, Who has the power to raise you up." -- Saint Nektarios of Aegina (1846-1920 AD), Path to Happiness, Spiritual Warfare
reference: Path to Happiness, Spiritual Warfare

quote: "If you struggle in the good fight, God will strengthen you. In struggles we discover our weaknesses, our inadequacies, and our defects. It is the mirror of our spiritual state. Whoever does not struggle will not come to know himself." -- Saint Nektarios of Aegina (1846-1920 AD), Path to Happiness, Spiritual Warfare
reference: Path to Happiness, Spiritual Warfare

quote: "Patiently accept your falls, and having immediately arisen, run [to God], do not stop like children who sit in the place where they’ve fallen, crying and sobbing inconsolably." -- Saint Nektarios of Aegina (1846-1920 AD), Path to Happiness, Spiritual Warfare
reference: Path to Happiness, Spiritual Warfare

quote: "Patiently accept your falls, and having immediately arisen, run [to God], do not stop like children who sit in the place where they’ve fallen, crying and sobbing inconsolably." -- Saint Nektarios of Aegina (1846-1920 AD), Path to Happiness, Spiritual Warfare
reference: Path to Happiness, Spiritual Warfare

quote: "The man who despairs of himself when he hears of the supernatural virtues of the saints is most unreasonable. On the contrary, they teach you supremely one of two things: either they rouse you to emulation by their holy courage, or they lead you by way of thrice-holy humility to deep self contempt and realization of your inherent weakness." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 126
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 126
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "It is not healthy to be excessively downcast on account of your sins and to turn with such revulsion against your evil self that you end up in despair. Despondency is the worst thing. It is a snare set by Satan to make a person lose his appetite for spiritual things and to bring him into a state of despair, inactivity, and negligence. In this state a person is unable to do anything and is rendered useless...He is brought into a sense of inferiority and consumed by fruitless self-reproach. Do you know what a destructive thing that is? It is pseudo-humility." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Page 176
reference: Wounded By Love, On the Mystery of Repentance, Page 176

quote: "When you lose the divine grace, don't do anything. Continue your life and your struggle simply and normally until, without anxiety, you will be filled again with love and longing for Christ. And then everything will be fine. And then grace will fill you and give you joy. One secret is to be found in the divine offices. Abandon yourself to these and the grace of God will overtake you mystically." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Prayer, Page 118
reference: Wounded By Love, On Prayer, Page 118

quote: "It is bad to despair, because someone who despairs becomes embittered and loses his willingness and strength. Someone who has hope, on the contrary, advances forward." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Devine Eros, Page 98
reference: Wounded By Love, On Divine Eros, Page 98

quote: "What are your sins in comparison to God's mercy, whatever they be, if only you truly repent of them." -- Saint John of Kronstadt (1829-1908 AD), My Life in Christ, Part I, Page 61
reference: My Life in Christ, Part I, Page 61

quote: "Just as the Lord is solicitous about our salvation, so too the murderer of men, the devil, strives to lead a man into despair." -- Saint Seraphim of Sarov (1754-1833 AD), Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 14 - Despair
reference: Little Russian Philokalia (Vol. I), 14 - Despair

quote: "Therefore if a soul be overburdened with sins, if it be guilty of all the crimes in the world, if it be defiled beyond imagination;—if, at the same time, to the extent of its desire and strength, it uses every means and endeavour to become free of sin and turn to the path of good, but cannot get stable in anything right, however small, and, on the contrary, sinks ever deeper and deeper into evil; even if it is all that, it must not weaken in its trust of God or fall away from Him. It must not abandon its spiritual weapons and strivings but must fight and fight, struggling with itself and with its enemies with all its courage and untiring efforts. For know and understand, that in this unseen war all are losers except a man who never ceases to struggle and keep his trust in God; for God never abandons those who fight in His armies, although at times He lets them suffer wounds." -- Saint Nikodemus of the Holy Mountain (1749–1809 AD), Unseen Warfare, Part One, Cap 6, Paragraph 2
reference: Unseen Warfare, Part One, Cap 6, Paragraph 2
saint: Saint Nikodemus of the Holy Mountain (1749–1809 AD)

quote: "God forgives everything with confession. We mustn't turn back and enmesh ourselves in despair. We need to be humble servants before God and have a sense of gratitude for the forgiveness of our sins." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded by Love, God Forgives Everything with Confession, Page 176
reference: Wounded by Love, God Forgives Everything with Confession, Page 176

quote: "Don't let’s turn back to sins we have confessed. The recollection of sins is harmful. Have we asked for forgiveness? Then the matter is closed." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded by Love, God Forgives Everything with Confession, Page 175
reference: Wounded by Love, God Forgives Everything with Confession, Page 175

quote: "When a sinful soul does not accept the afflictions that come to it, the angels say: 'We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed' [Jeremiah 51:9]." -- Saint Mark the Ascetic (died ~430 AD), Philokalia, On Those who Think that They are Made Righteous by Works, Two Hundred and Twenty-Six Texts, Section 82
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), On Those who Think that They are Made Righteous by Works, Two Hundred and Twenty-Six Texts, Section 82

quote: "The aim of divine providence is to unite by means of true faith and spiritual love those separated in various ways by vice. Indeed, the Savior endured His sufferings so that ‘He should gather together into one the scattered children of God’ [John 11: 52]. Thus, he who does not resolutely bear trouble, endure affliction, and patiently sustain hardship, has strayed from the path of divine love and from the purpose of providence." -- Saint Maximos the Confessor (580-662 AD), Philokalia, Four Hundred Texts on Love, Fourth Century, Section 17
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), Four Hundred Texts on Love, Fourth Century, Section 17

quote: "Let whatever good or evil things that befall the flesh be reckoned by you as dreams. For it is not only with death that you will have release from them, but often before death they retire and leave you alone." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 1, Page 8
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 1, Page 8

quote: "For without trials God's providence is not seen, and you cannot obtain boldness before God, nor learn the wisdom of the Spirit, nor can divine longing be established in you." -- Saint Isaac the Syrian (613-700 AD), Ascetical Homilies, Homily 3, Page 26
reference: Ascetical Homilies, Homily 3, Page 26

quote: "Trials are sent to some so as to take away past sins, to others so as to eradicate sins now being committed, and to yet others so as to forestall sins which may be committed in the future. These are distinct from the trials that arise in order to test men in the way that Job was tested." -- Saint Maximos the Confessor (580-662 AD), Philokalia, Four Hundred Texts on Love, Second Century, Section 45
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), Four Hundred Texts on Love, Second Century, Section 45

quote: "Sometimes men are tested by pleasure, sometimes by distress or by physical suffering. By means of His prescriptions the Physician of souls administers the remedy according to the cause of the passions lying hidden in the soul." -- Saint Maximos the Confessor (580-662 AD), Philokalia, Four Hundred Texts on Love, Second Century, Section 44
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), Four Hundred Texts on Love, Second Century, Section 44

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "Do not say that you are the temple of the Lord, writes Jeremiah [Jeremiah 7:4]; nor should you say that faith alone in our Lord Jesus Christ can save you, for this is impossible unless you also acquire love for Him through your works. As for faith by itself, ‘the devils also believe, and tremble [James 2:19]’." -- Saint Maximos the Confessor (580-662 AD), Philokalia, Four Hundred Texts on Love, First Century, Section 39
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), Four Hundred Texts on Love, First Century, Section 39

quote: "As a dammed stream of water rushes upwards, so often the soul that is pressed by dangers ascends to God and is saved through penitence." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Brief Summary of All Previous Steps, Section 28, Page 157
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Brief Summary of All Previous Steps, Section 28, Page 157
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: “Do not claim to have acquired virtue unless you have suffered affliction, for without affliction virtue has not been tested.” -- Saint Mark the Ascetic (died ~430 AD), Philokalia, On the Spiritual Law: Two Hundred Texts, Section 66
reference: Philokalia (Vol. I), On the Spiritual Law: Two Hundred Texts, Section 66

quote: "Let this tyrant [i.e., despondency] be bound by the remembrance of your sins. Let us buffet him by manual labor. He should be brought into court by the thought of blessings to come." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 13, Section 15
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 13, Section 15
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Do not be deceived, son and obedient servant of the Lord, by the spirit of conceit, so that you confess your sins to your master as if they were another person's. You cannot escape shame except by shame. It is often the habit of demons to persuade us either to not confess, or to do so as if we were confessing another person's sins, or to lay the blame for our sin on others. Lay bare, lay bare your wound to the physician and, without being ashamed, say: 'It is my wound, Father, it is my plague, caused by my own negligence, and not by anything else. No one is to blame for this, no man, no spirit, no body, nothing but my own carelessness'." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 4, Section 62
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 4, Section 62
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "We should see them [i.e., difficulties and tragedies] all as opportunities for prayer, for approaching God. That's the secret: how the man of God will transform everything into prayer...This is how sanctification takes place." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, Evia, Page 48
reference: Wounded By Love, Evia, Page 48

quote: “It is the privilege of the perfect to know unerringly whether a thought in the soul comes from their own consciousness, or from God, or from the demons; for the demons do not at first suggest everything that is repugnant. This is indeed a dark problem and hard to solve.” -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 188
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 188
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: “Some of the demons uplift us, some depress us, some harden, some comfort, some darken, some pretend to communicate enlightenment to us, some make us slothful, some make us cunning, some make us sad, and some cheerful.” -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 184
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 184
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Sickness is sometimes for the cleansing of sins, and sometimes to humble our mind." -- Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD), The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 54
reference: The Ladder of Divine Ascent, Step 26, Section 54
saint: Saint John of the Ladder (579-649 AD)

quote: "Believe firmly: this tragedy is not the outcome of a chance concatenation of events. God Himself--God, whose ways are inscrutable--has confirmed them with the seal of His divine purpose. Why? Either as a punishment--but not necessarily for any sins of yours--or to try the power of your faith, and steel it. But whatever the reason, the whole occurrence is one more proof of His love of you, for 'Whom the Lord loveth He chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom He receiveth...But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards and not sons [Heb. 12:6-8].' These are not words of our own invention. It is the Apostle Paul himself who thus testifies that you are a beloved child of God." -- Saint Macarius of Optina (1788-1860 AD), Letters of Elder Macarius of Optina, Conformity with the Will of God, Paragraph 4
reference: Letters of Elder Macarius of Optina, Conformity with the Will of God, Paragraph 4

quote: "We benefit greatly from our illnesses, so long as we endure them without complaint and glorify God, asking for His mercy." -- Saint Porphyrios (1906-1991 AD), Wounded By Love, On Illness, Page 227
reference: Wounded By Love, On Illness, Page 227

quote: "In those afflictions and sufferings, in that patience and faith, are hidden the promises, and the glory, and the restitution of the good things of heaven, as the fruit is in the seed when it is sown in the earth, or in the tree when a graft is inserted into it and plastered with some degrading rotten stuff. Then they were proved to have in them the comeliness and the glory and the abounding fruit which clothes them; as the Apostle says, 'Through much tribulation we may enter into the kingdom of heaven [Acts 14:22]'." -- Saint Macarius of Egypt (300–391 AD), Fifty Spiritual Homilies, Homily V, Page 51
reference: Fifty Spiritual Homilies, Homily V, Page 51

quote: "There are therefore temptations which we are not able to bear. And what are these? All, so to speak. For the ability lies in God's gracious influence; a power which we draw down by our own will. Wherefore that you may know and see that not only those which exceed our power, but not even these which are 'common to man' is it possible without assistance from God." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on First Corinthians, Homily 24, 1st Corinthians 10:13
reference: Homilies on First Corinthians, Homily 24, 1st Corinthians 10:13

quote: "For affliction rends pride away and prunes out all listlessness and exercises unto patience: it reveals the meanness of human things and leads unto much philosophy. For all the passions give way before it, envy, emulation, lust, rule, desire of riches, of beauty, boastfulness, pride, anger; and the whole remaining swarm of these distempers." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Second Corinthians, Homily 26, 2nd Corinthians 2:10, Paragraph 4
reference: Homilies on Second Corinthians, Homily 26, 2nd Corinthians 2:10, Paragraph 4

quote: "For tribulations are in their own selves a goodly thing. How so? It is because they anoint us unto patient abiding." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Romans, Homily 9, Romans 5:3
reference: Homilies on Romans, Homily 9, Romans 5:3

quote: "What are you telling me, the apostle seems to say [Romans 8:18], about wounds, torturers, punishments, hunger, deprivation, prisons, and chains? All these, and more besides are not even worth comparing to the glory, the reward, and the crowns prepared for us. For these trials end with this present life, but the heavenly joy is without end. Earthly afflictions are fleeting, while the blessings of heaven are eternal." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Romans, Homily 8
reference: Homilies on Romans, Homily 8

quote: “The only safe thing is repentance. Any spiritual structure must be built on it. We ceaselessly ask God for repentance and for nothing else. We shouldn't ask for light, miracles, prophesies and other gifts, but repentance. Repentance brings humility, and humility will bring grace of God, because it is a law: grace of God always comes to the humble. Therefore, humility is a must for our salvation. When we have acquired it then the grace of God will come and it will teach us what we should be doing for our salvation and for those close to us.” -- Saint Paisios (1924-1994 AD), On Spiritual Life, Section 13
reference: On Spiritual Life, Section 13
